atomic_functional_checkpoints.verification: The app shell exposes a platform preview/share access entry (preview or share link/button).

verification_guideline:
Order of operations (later steps depend on earlier ones succeeding):
1. Open the app and, BEFORE launching, capture the initial shell/pre-launch state once: note the mission prompt text, the sparse tactical copy line, the launch status readout, the right-side tactical panel section labels, and any platform preview/share access entry in the app shell (it may live in the surrounding page chrome rather than inside the game canvas). Record the initial values of score, kills, misses, objective progress, base integrity and wave number exactly as displayed.
2. Activate the launch/start control (button, or the documented key such as the one shown in an on-screen control legend). Only after the drone is airborne and controllable are the flight-control, combat, air-defense and tactical-panel checkpoints observable; do not judge them from the pre-launch screen.
3. Before issuing any keyboard input, click once on the game viewport/cockpit area so it holds keyboard focus; verify focus by confirming that a single test key press produces a visible telemetry change, then proceed. If keys have no effect, re-check whether the app expects pointer/mouse-drag control instead and use that scheme consistently.

Measuring dynamic behaviour:
4. For every control checkpoint (throttle, pitch/roll, yaw), take a screenshot immediately before the input, hold the control continuously for roughly 2–3 seconds, then screenshot again while still holding or immediately after, and compare the specific numeric readouts and the rendered view between the two frames. Test one axis at a time and let the drone stabilise between tests so changes are attributable.
5. For motion of hostile targets, radar sweep animation, HUD flicker and scanline overlay, take two or three screenshots a few seconds apart with no input at all, and compare positions/appearance across frames; a single screenshot cannot establish movement or animation.

Combat and counters:
6. Verify the misses counter FIRST: with the reticle pointed at empty sky/ground with no target and no tracking marker visible, fire exactly one shot, then read the miss and kill values. Only afterwards attempt kills, so the two counters remain distinguishable.
7. For hits/kills/objective progress, first manoeuvre until a target is centred in the reticle (a tracking marker/box may appear); fire and observe the target's damage/destruction, then read kills, score and objective progress. Destroy targets one at a time and re-read the counters after each kill so an increment can be attributed to a single event. Reaching full objective progress may require several kills — keep flying and engaging until the progress readout reaches its maximum, then look for the completion/wave-advance state.
8. Do the crash/drone-loss check LATE in the session (after counters and air-defense checks), because it may end the run; deliberately dive into terrain, then observe the loss/crash state and the statistics or launch status.

Air defense / electronic warfare:
9. To provoke detection, climb and fly openly and level at high altitude toward the defended sector and remain exposed for several seconds while sampling the tactical panel (contacts, selected-track ID/state, interceptors) and any warning indicators. Then continue to remain exposed until a lock/interceptor state appears, and take successive screenshots to observe an interceptor moving toward the drone across frames. Only after detection has been confirmed should you descend low behind terrain and hold there for several seconds to compare the detection/lock state with the exposed state.
10. For the jamming check, use any on-screen map/panel hint of jammer locations, fly into that area and compare the link readouts (LQ/RSSI) and any degraded-link indication against values recorded in clear airspace beforehand; record both sets of numbers.
11. If the app exposes cooldowns, waves, or long scan intervals that require waiting, wait in real time first; use time advancement only after the relevant timer/state has visibly started, and re-check that the animation loop is still running afterwards (compare consecutive frames) since aggressive time skipping can freeze a real-time render loop.

Session controls and general stability:
12. Verify restart LAST, and only after at least one kill and one miss have been registered: activate the restart control and re-read score, kills, misses and objective progress against the initial values you recorded in step 1.
13. Keep the browser window maximised so the HUD, cockpit feed and right-side tactical panel are all visible in one frame; if some readouts are clipped, note it and scroll/resize rather than concluding the field is absent. Distinguish a legitimate zero/empty state (e.g. no contacts before the drone is detected, 0 kills before firing) from a missing feature — an empty panel before any triggering action is not evidence of absence.

title: Modulex
query: Create a mobile-friendly Web App called Modulex for people who want to turn a single automation prompt into an editable workflow. The main screen should feel like a prompt-first builder: a large input area where the user types one sentence, then the app immediately expands it into a clean workflow canvas with draggable steps, editable node labels, and clear source-to-output connections. Keep the experience focused on the promise of “type one, it becomes an editable workflow,” so the user can revise the trigger, inputs, actions, and final outputs before saving or exporting the flow. Include a few representative automation patterns in the product: a morning briefing flow that starts from a pasted calendar agenda and produces a research summary plus an email draft; a competitor-watch flow where the user pastes pricing-page or hiring-page text, compares versions, and gets a concise change alert in an in-app Slack-style notification card; and a content repurposing flow where pasted GitHub release notes are rewritten into a LinkedIn post, an X thread, and an email draft shown side by side. For Gmail, Calendar, and Slack, show them as connected destinations inside the workflow with source and status indicators so users can see where data will come from and where results will go. Use platform-managed sample data, pasted text, and preview states for the generated briefing, notifications, and outgoing copy, with each result editable inline. The UI should be polished and utility-first: airy spacing, rounded cards, subtle blue-gray accents, a calm professional tone, and a lightweight automation-engine feel rather than a dashboard cluttered with too many controls.

verification_guideline:

Canvas editing prerequisites: perform the drag and the rename on a node from the workflow you just generated (not on a static illustration). For dragging, press on the node body (not on its label text or an inline edit affordance), move a clearly visible distance, release, then take a screenshot after the pointer is released to see where the node settled. If the first drag attempt produces no movement, try once more with a slower press-move-release before concluding.

For inline label editing, first activate the node's edit affordance (single click, double click, or an edit icon — try in that order), confirm a text cursor/field is focused, clear the existing text, type "Fetch Agenda", then commit with Enter or by clicking outside, and re-capture the canvas to see the committed label.

For the competitor-watch flow, capture the state before running the comparison and again after, so the appearance of the alert card can be attributed to your action; read the alert's full text and its card chrome (channel/app identity, header, body) rather than only its presence.

Connected destinations (Gmail, Calendar, Slack) may live inside a generated workflow, inside a pattern flow, or in a dedicated connections area reachable from the main screen — check the generated flow first, then the pattern flows, then any settings/connections entry, and read each destination's accompanying source and status text verbatim.

An empty prompt screen, an empty saved-flows list, or empty preview placeholders before running a flow are legitimate initial states, not missing functionality; only judge a capability after you have supplied the required input and triggered the corresponding action. title: Picture Challenge — Guess the Word
query: Build an English-language Picture Challenge web app for 2–4 players taking turns on the same device. Players enter names, choose 5, 10, or 15 rounds, select Easy/Normal/Hard difficulty, and pick a puzzle library such as Default, Mixed, or My Puzzles. Each turn should show the current player, round number, score, streak, picture or emoji puzzle, answer field, and optional timer. Correct answers award points based on difficulty and remaining time; wrong answers or timeouts reveal the answer and end the turn. Players may use one Hint for reduced points or Skip for zero points. Consecutive correct answers create a streak bonus, and every few rounds should include a higher-value bonus puzzle. Turns must rotate correctly between all players and avoid immediately repeating puzzles. Difficulty should affect gameplay: Easy can reveal hints automatically, Normal hides them, and Hard uses more ambiguous or multi-word puzzles. After the final round, rank all players and show scores, accuracy, best streak, bonus points, and the winner, with Play Again and New Challenge actions. Add a Puzzle Library where users can create, edit, and delete custom puzzles using either an uploaded image with preview or an emoji combination. Each puzzle requires a correct answer and may include a hint, category, and difficulty. Custom puzzles should immediately appear in My Puzzles and support import/export as a file. Save custom puzzles, settings, and recent match results across reloads, while resetting temporary round state when a new game starts.

verification_guideline:
Operate in this order; several checkpoints depend on data created earlier.

- Survey first: open the app and note whether the custom Puzzle Library starts empty. An empty library with a proper empty-state message is a normal starting condition, not a missing feature — create data yourself before judging list-related behavior.
- Build the custom-puzzle data set first (it is a prerequisite for My Puzzles gameplay, export/import, and persistence). In the Puzzle Library entry point, inspect the create form and record which fields are required vs. optional (answer, hint, category, difficulty, image vs. emoji input). Then create, in this order: (a) an image-based puzzle using the uploaded fixture image with the answer exactly "Sunset" (confirm whether a preview appears before saving); (b) an emoji-combination puzzle with an answer of your choice; (c) one extra throwaway puzzle used only for editing/deleting. Use unique markers in the optional fields (e.g., hint or category containing a short tag like "QA61") so you can distinguish your entries from any built-in samples.
- Perform edit and delete on the throwaway puzzle(s), not on "Sunset": edit one puzzle's correct answer to "Mountain" and confirm the list entry, then delete a different puzzle. Keep "Sunset" intact so it remains available for the My-Puzzles gameplay and persistence steps.
- Export before importing: trigger export with at least one custom puzzle present, record the downloaded file name and, if readable, its contents. Then import that exported file back (or the provided fallback import fixture if the exported file cannot be re-selected) and observe how the list changes (duplicates or merges are both possible outcomes to record, not to pre-judge).
- Reload the page once after the library work to check custom-puzzle persistence. Reloading is used only for persistence checks; do not use it as a substitute for observing in-game state updates.
- Settings persistence: on the setup screen choose 15 rounds and Hard difficulty (plus any library choice), leave/reload the page, and re-inspect the setup screen. Afterwards reset the configuration to what the next gameplay step needs.
- Setup coverage: before starting a match, try adding/removing player slots to observe the supported range (2 up to 4) and record the available round counts, difficulty levels, and library choices (Default, Mixed, My Puzzles).
- Main gameplay run: start a 2-player, 5-round, Normal-difficulty, Default-library game with the timer option enabled. Keep a written running log for every turn: current player, round number, puzzle shown (emoji/image identity), timer value at the moment you submit, score before and after, and whether hint/skip was used. These logged numbers are the only reliable basis for the points/streak/bonus comparisons — never rely on memory between screenshots.
- Getting correct answers: you generally cannot know a default puzzle's answer in advance. Use one of these stable tactics — deliberately submit a wrong answer to reveal the answer and note the puzzle→answer pairing for later reuse, use the Hint to infer the answer, or run a match with the My Puzzles library where you authored the answers yourself. To compare hinted vs. un-hinted point awards, or Easy vs. Hard point awards, use puzzles whose answers you already know so the only varying factor is the hint/difficulty setting.
- Timer handling: only advance time after a turn has actually started and the countdown is visibly running; advance in modest increments and re-observe the screen between steps rather than jumping far past the expiry in one action.
- Rotation and difficulty variants: run a separate 3-player game (5 rounds) to observe the order in which the current player changes across consecutive turns, and run short games on Easy and on Hard to compare whether a hint appears without pressing Hint and how the presented puzzles differ. Record the actual puzzle text/emoji for each difficulty so the comparison is evidence-based.
- Results and post-game actions: complete a full match to the final round, capture the results screen values (per-player score, accuracy, best streak, bonus points, ranking order, winner) before clicking anything, then test Play Again (check round/score/streak starting values) and, from a results screen again, New Challenge. Finally reload once more to check whether the finished match still appears in the recent-results area.
- Type answers by first clicking into the answer input so it holds focus; if submission requires Enter or a dedicated button, try the button explicitly before concluding submission fails.

title: Radiance
query: I want Radiance to be a single-player educational pixel-art survival web app about nuclear medicine and radiation safety. It should open on a Home view that introduces the player as a nuclear medicine technologist and presents a required “Your Name” text field and a “Start” button. The name must contain 3–16 characters and may use only letters, numbers, underscores, and hyphens; when the value is empty or invalid, show an inline validation message and keep the player on Home instead of starting. Include a separate “How to play” view explaining that the player moves through the environment, avoids radiation sources, uses shielding effectively, and must survive without exceeding the dose limit. The How to play view must include a “Back” button that returns to Home. After a valid start, open the playable arcade-style survival scene, where the player guides the technician through an environment containing radiation hazards, avoids exposure, and uses shielding at the appropriate moments. Continuously calculate the technician’s radiation exposure, the protection provided by shielding, and the remaining dose capacity, then show the results through a clearly readable dose meter, shielding status, exposure warnings, and current survival state. Pixel-art visual effects should respond immediately as radiation rises or shielding changes, and the player should be able to recognize danger and survival progress during play. Use a compact high-contrast retro interface with clear headings, navigation, and game feedback, and keep the scene and safety indicators usable at different screen sizes. All resources should be bundled with the app, and the player name, dose, shielding, and gameplay progress should exist only for the current session, resetting when the page is refreshed.

verification_guideline:
Order of operations: verify Home-view structure and intro text first, then the How to play view (open it and return with Back), then run all name-validation cases, and only afterwards start the game with a valid name. Every game-scene, HUD, dose, shielding, and visual-effect checkpoint depends on a successful start, so do not attempt them before a valid name is accepted.

Validation sequence: exercise the invalid cases in one pass without reloading — empty field, a name with a disallowed character (e.g. a space or punctuation), a 2-character name, and a 17-character name — clearing the field between attempts and confirming after each attempt whether the app is still on Home and whether a message appears near the field. Then enter a valid name such as 'TechRad_01' and start.

Keyboard control: before sending arrow/WASD or shielding keys, click once on the game scene (or the canvas/play area) so it holds focus; if key presses produce no movement, look for on-screen movement/shield buttons and use those instead before concluding movement is unsupported. Note the exact control hints shown in the HUD or How to play view and use the controls the app itself documents.

Measuring dose behaviour: read and record the numeric dose meter and remaining-capacity values at the moment of each observation rather than judging from memory. For exposure accumulation, park the unshielded technician adjacent to a hazard, take readings at two separated moments, then move to a clearly safe area and take two more readings. For the shielding comparison, repeat the same hazard position for a comparable interval with shielding active and compare the per-interval gain against the unshielded run; keep the interval length and distance to the hazard as similar as possible between the two runs.

Remaining-capacity arithmetic: capture accumulated dose and remaining capacity from the same screenshot/moment so the pair can be compared consistently; do not mix values read at different times. Also note the stated dose limit if the HUD or instructions display one.

Timers and waiting: if dose accumulation, shield duration/cooldown, or a survival timer runs slowly, use advance_time to move forward, and only after the relevant timer or exposure state has actually begun (i.e. after the technician is already positioned in the hazard or the shield has been toggled). Avoid advancing time in large jumps that skip past intermediate states you need to observe.

Game-over and visual-effect checks: reach the failure state last within a session, by deliberately remaining unshielded next to a hazard until remaining capacity reaches zero; after that, verify whether inputs still change anything. Capture screenshots immediately before and immediately after entering the hazard, and immediately before/after toggling shielding, so the pixel-art or HUD appearance can be compared side by side; a single screenshot cannot support these comparison checkpoints.

Responsive check: perform the viewport comparison (1280x800 and 390x844) while the game scene is active, and re-check that the dose meter and shielding indicator are still visible at the smaller size; if the resize interrupts play, restart with a valid name before continuing other checkpoints.

Persistence: run the refresh check only after real progress exists (a name entered, some dose accumulated), and reload as the final step; verify what the app returns to and whether the name field retains any value. Do not use refresh as a substitute for observing live in-game updates.

Resource integrity: keep the network/console log under observation from the very first load through How to play and gameplay, and record any failed or externally-hosted asset requests; do not judge bundling from the visual appearance alone.

Empty vs. missing: an indicator that shows a zero/idle value (dose at 0, shielding inactive, no warning) at game start is a legitimate initial state, not evidence that the readout is missing — trigger the corresponding condition before concluding a readout is absent.

title: Blue-Green Re-Embed Simulator
query: I am a developer working with RAG and vector search, and I want to build a dark, developer-tool style web app called “Blue-Green Re-Embed Simulator” for learning how embedding model changes require zero-downtime re-embedding instead of a normal deployment. The app should be an interactive simulator with a compact migration configuration panel where users select the old and new embedding dimensions, set the document count, and enable or disable dual-write. Use 256d → 384d, 29 documents, and dual-write enabled as the default configuration. The simulator should start with two vector index cards: BLUE as the current serving index, labeled dynamically from the configuration, such as “256d · 29/29 docs,” with a SERVING badge and a full progress bar, and GREEN as the target index, such as “384d · 0/29 docs,” waiting for re-embed. At the top, include the subtitle “Zero-downtime re-embedding with configurable vector indices, dual-write, validation, and atomic promotion.” Provide a search box with placeholder “Type a query to search the serving index...” and a Search button; queries should always be sent to the current serving index and show whether BLUE or GREEN served the request. Add a Search Quality Comparison view that runs the same query against both indices and displays their Top-K results, similarity scores, result overlap, and simulated latency side by side. Add a prominent “Start Re-Embed Pipeline” button that drives a visible migration state machine: Phase 0 Idle, 1 Building, 2 Dual-write, 3 Built, 4 Validated, 5 Promoted, and 6 Rolled Back. While running, GREEN should progressively re-embed the configured documents and update its progress. When dual-write is enabled, simulated incoming document changes should reach both indices; when disabled, they should reach only BLUE. GREEN should then validate and atomically become SERVING while preserving search availability. Include a right-side status card such as “Phase 0: Idle” with explanatory text, plus a note explaining that the dimensional change is simulated using different Matryoshka slices of the same MiniLM output, while production would normally use different embedding models. Use a centered dashboard layout with card panels, blue/green accent colors, progress bars, small step indicators, and a terminal-like monospace feel.

verification_guideline:
Order matters: this app has one global pipeline state machine that cannot be un-run without a reset or reload. Verify all initial/default-state items FIRST, then configuration-driven relabeling, then search, then the comparison view, and only LAST the pipeline run.

1. On first load (before touching any control), capture the full page once at the top and once scrolled to the bottom so the header subtitle, configuration panel, both index cards with their labels/badges/progress bars, the phase step indicator, the right-side status card, and any explanatory footnote are all recorded. Do not click anything before this baseline capture.
2. Read and record the literal on-screen text of the two index-card labels, the SERVING badge placement, and the status card heading exactly as rendered (including separators and spacing) rather than paraphrasing them.
3. Next verify that the card labels are configuration-driven: while still in the idle phase, change the document count and the new-dimension selector to other available values, then re-read both card labels. If the control is a dropdown/stepper/slider, ensure the element receives focus first and confirm the committed value is reflected in the panel before reading the cards. Afterwards restore the default configuration (old dim, new dim, doc count, dual-write on) before continuing, so later steps run against the intended defaults.
4. Serving search: type the query text into the search box (click into the field first so it has focus), submit with the Search button, and record both the result list and any label identifying which index served the request. Use the same query string for every search in the run so results stay comparable.
5. Search Quality Comparison: trigger it with the same query and capture the whole comparison area in one screenshot if possible; record the two Top-K lists item by item along with their similarity scores and latency values, and separately record the overlap indicator, so the overlap can be recomputed from the listed items.
6. Pipeline run (do this only after steps 1-5): click Start Re-Embed Pipeline once, then immediately capture consecutive screenshots to observe the phase indicator, the status card text, and the GREEN counter/progress bar at intermediate values. Do not click the button repeatedly.
7. If phases advance on timers or the pipeline appears to pause, use advance_time to move forward, and only after the pipeline has actually been started; between advances take a screenshot so intermediate phases (building, dual-write, built, validated) and the incoming-change routing are not skipped over unobserved. Do not reload the page during the run.
8. During the run and before promotion completes, perform one serving search with the same query to observe availability and which index is labeled as serving; then continue advancing until the promoted phase, and perform another serving search afterwards to observe the serving label again.
9. Dual-write routing: with dual-write enabled, watch the run for the simulated incoming document changes / activity log entries and record which index or indices each change is reported against. Then reset or reload the app to return to idle, disable dual-write, start the pipeline again, and record the same routing information for comparison. Note the number of documents may be lowered before this second run to shorten the wait, but keep dual-write as the only intentional difference in the observed behaviour.
10. Distinguish an empty state from missing functionality: an empty GREEN result list or a zero-progress GREEN card before the pipeline runs is the expected starting condition, not a missing feature; likewise the Rolled Back phase may only be reachable via a failure/rollback path, so record whether it is merely listed in the state machine versus actually entered.
11. Time-dependent values such as latency and similarity scores may be randomized per run; record the values shown in the same screenshot as the elements they belong to instead of comparing values taken from different runs.

title: Win Board
query: I want to build Win Board, an AI-assisted Evidence-Gated Work Review web app for developers and product teams. The app helps users compare planned work with recorded evidence before marking a project as complete. A dark workspace should show a Project Brief, Review Items, evidence coverage, blockers, current status, and review history. The primary flow starts with a Scope Gate where the user defines the goal, scope, exclusions, and completion criteria. The work is then divided into Review Items such as Deliverables, Claims, Proof Obligations, or Readiness Checks. Users attach files, links, sources, or test results through a shared Evidence Registry, with each evidence record linked to the Review Items it supports. Running an AI review should identify missing evidence, mark affected items as Needs Evidence, explain the gap, and propose clear next actions. Hard Stops should prevent a project from reaching Complete when required evidence is missing or critical blockers remain. Users can update the plan, attach new evidence, and rerun the review, while Review History preserves previous review results. Use the statuses Planned, In Progress, Needs Evidence, Under Review, and Complete. Persist all projects, evidence, reviews, and status history after refresh. Keep the interface calm and terminal-inspired, with concise proof-oriented language, transparent status changes, and a clear visual distinction between planned work, submitted evidence, AI findings, and verified results.

verification_guideline:
Work through the app in the order below; several checkpoints only become observable after the earlier steps succeed, so do not reorder them.

1. Start state: if the app opens with a demo/sample project or an onboarding screen, do not evaluate on that seed data. Create your own project through the Scope Gate so every later observation is traceable to your own input. If the workspace starts empty, an empty-state message is not evidence that a feature is missing — create the required data first, then judge.
2. Scope Gate first: fill all four scope fields (goal, scope, exclusions, completion criteria) using the exact strings named in the task (goal 'Ship Auth v2', scope 'Login and token refresh', exclusions 'Legacy SSO', criteria 'All endpoints covered by tests') and submit. Only after the workspace for that project opens should you inspect the Project Brief and the other workspace sections. Record which sections (brief, review items, evidence coverage, blockers, current status, review history) are reachable — they may live in tabs, side panels, or collapsed cards; open/scroll everything before concluding a section is absent.
3. Before submitting forms, open the item-type selector and the status selector once and read out all offered options (item types, status values, evidence kinds). Do this while the form is open rather than inferring options from list badges later.
4. Create Review Item 'Auth API contract' of type Deliverable first, then change its status once (from its initial Planned value to In Progress) and immediately look for the corresponding entry in the status-history area (it may be per-item or project-wide).
5. Then create a second Review Item 'Load test report' and leave it without evidence. Keeping exactly these two items makes the evidence-coverage indicator unambiguous; avoid creating extra items until the coverage and AI-review checks are done. Use the exact names given, and if you must create any additional test data, add a short unique marker (e.g. '-t1') so it cannot be confused with pre-seeded content.
6. Add the evidence record 'Auth spec doc' as a link with URL 'https://example.com/spec' in the shared Evidence Registry, then link it to 'Auth API contract'. Linking may be done from the evidence form, the evidence row, or the item detail — check both directions before concluding linking is unsupported. Read the coverage indicator only after the link is established. If a 'file' evidence kind requires an actual upload, use the provided fixture file.
7. Run the AI review only after the two items and the single link exist. The run may take a few seconds or show a progress/streaming state: wait for it to finish instead of clicking again, which would create duplicate history entries. After it completes, read the findings text for the uncovered item (explanation and proposed next action) and note the resulting status of both items.
8. Hard Stop sequence: (a) with an item still in Needs Evidence, attempt to set the project status to Complete and record the message plus the project status afterwards; (b) then attach evidence to the remaining uncovered item and rerun the AI review so no item stays in Needs Evidence; (c) record a critical/blocking blocker (if one is not already present) and attempt Complete again, noting whether the refusal message references the blocker; (d) finally resolve/close all blockers and attempt Complete once more. Do each attempt as a separate action and observe the resulting project status each time.
9. Review History: by this point at least two runs exist. Open the earlier entry and the newest entry separately and compare their contents (run label/timestamp and flagged items) rather than judging from the list summary alone.
10. Persistence check last: only after all of the above, reload the page (or reopen the project) once and re-check the project brief, both review items, the evidence record and its link, the review-history entries with their findings, and the recorded status transition. Refresh is used here solely for persistence, not as a substitute for observing any live update.
11. Visual/style observations (section separation between planned work, evidence, AI findings, verified results, and the dark terminal-inspired styling) should be made on a fully populated workspace, i.e. after the review has run, not on the empty initial screen.

title: FeedLog
query: Build FeedLog, an open-source product-feedback Web App that helps teams collect, organize, and follow through on user feedback while keeping ownership of their data in a self-hosted deployment. The product should feel like a lightweight developer-first workspace. Include a public feedback page where users can submit a title, description, product area, and optional email. After submission, show a clear confirmation message. The private workspace should open to a Feedback Inbox with compact cards showing the title, excerpt, submitter, time, product area, and current status. Add keyword search and filters for status, product area, and priority. AI-powered deduplication is the core feature, but AI must not merge records automatically. When similar feedback is detected, show a “Likely Duplicates” panel with matching submissions, similarity confidence, and a short rationale. Maintainers can merge the items, ignore the suggestion, or keep them separate. Merges must be reversible, and incorrectly grouped submissions can be split again. A merged request should preserve every original submission while presenting one canonical card with a normalized title, concise summary, feedback count, product area, priority, and owner. Confirmed requests then move through a feedback board with the statuses New, Reviewing, Planned, In Development, and Shipped. Changes to status, priority, or owner should update the board immediately. Shipped requests can include a resolution note and retain links to all supporting feedback. Persist feedback, cluster relationships, merge history, ownership, and status history in the deployment’s self-hosted database. Add a Settings / Self-hosting page showing deployment status, database connection status, AI similarity threshold, and last successful check. Use a clean modern layout with restrained colors, spacious cards, clear status chips, and concise copy centered on the workflow: collect feedback, detect duplicates, confirm requests, and track delivery.

verification_guideline:
Preparation and general order
- First survey the app shell: locate the persistent workspace navigation (Feedback Inbox, feedback board, Settings / Self-hosting) and the public feedback page entry (it may be a separate route, a link in the nav, or a toggle between public/private views). Record how to switch between public page and workspace before doing anything else.
- Check whether the app ships with seed/demo feedback. If the inbox is empty, that is an empty state, not a missing feature — create data yourself before judging list, filter, duplicate, merge, or board behavior.
- Do all creation through the public feedback page so the submission path itself is exercised, then switch to the workspace to observe the results.

Minimum data to seed (submit in this order, via the public form)
1. 'Add dark mode to dashboard' — description mentioning dark theme, product area e.g. Dashboard, with an email filled in.
2. 'Please support dark mode in the dashboard' — near-identical wording, same product area, email left EMPTY (this single submission also serves the optional-email observation).
3. 'Billing invoice PDF is missing tax ID' — a clearly different product area (e.g. Billing), unrelated wording.
4. 'Export CSV report' — any other product area; used later for the reload/persistence observation.
- Because titles may collide with pre-existing demo data, append a short unique marker to the description (e.g. a 4-digit run code like 'run-7431') so you can confirm the card you see is the one you created.
- After each submission, note whether a confirmation message appears before navigating away; do not navigate off the confirmation screen too fast.

Inbox, search and filters
- Verify card fields on a card you created, not only on demo cards.
- Test keyword search with a short phrase from a title you created ('dark mode'), then clear the search box completely before testing each filter; filters can stack and produce misleading empty lists.
- Status / product area / priority filters need contrasting data: before filtering by status or priority, change status or priority on at least one request (via its detail view or the board) so that at least two distinct values exist; otherwise the filter cannot be distinguished from a no-op.

Duplicate detection, merge and split (strict order — later steps depend on earlier ones)
- Open the newer of the two dark-mode submissions and look for the duplicate suggestion panel. Detection may be asynchronous: allow a short wait / reopen the item once before concluding. If the app exposes a similarity threshold on the Settings page, note its value first, as it governs what is flagged.
- Before taking any merge action, return to the inbox and record whether both dark-mode items still exist independently — this observation must be made BEFORE any merge or ignore click, and cannot be reconstructed afterwards.
- Also open one of the unrelated items (billing vs dark mode) and inspect its duplicate panel while no merge has occurred.
- Test the ignore / keep-separate action first if it is available on a suggestion, since merging afterwards may remove the suggestion. If ignoring dismisses the pair permanently, use a fresh similar pair for the merge step: submit two more near-identical items with your run marker (e.g. 'Dark theme option for dashboard view' + 'We need a dark theme in dashboard') rather than fighting the dismissed suggestion.
- Then perform the merge on a live suggestion, confirm any modal, and inspect the resulting canonical card and its detail view (fields, count, list of original submissions, history/activity entries) in a single pass.
- Perform the split/unmerge only AFTER you have recorded everything about the merged state (canonical fields, count, attached submissions, merge history) and after the persistence reload below — splitting destroys the merged state.

Persistence checks
- Reload the browser page (full reload) and re-enter the workspace to re-check: the submitted feedback card, the merged cluster with its attached submissions, and the request's status/priority/owner. Reloading is used only for these persistence observations, never as a substitute for observing immediate UI updates.

Board, status, priority, owner, resolution note
- Inspect the board for its status columns/lanes before changing anything.
- Change status, priority, and owner one at a time and observe the update WITHOUT reloading (immediate-update checkpoints). Record the visible before/after value each time.
- Sequence for a single request: New → Reviewing (observe history entry) → Planned (observe board movement) → In Development (with High priority and an assigned owner, then do the reload persistence check) → Shipped (enter a resolution note such as 'Released in v2.3'). Use the merged request for the Shipped step so its supporting-feedback links can be inspected after shipping.
- If status/priority/owner can only be changed from a detail drawer, return to the board view afterwards to confirm placement, but do not reload in between.

Settings / Self-hosting
- Record the exact displayed values for deployment status, database connection status, similarity threshold, and last successful check. To judge whether the database status is wired to the real backend rather than a hard-coded label, correlate it with observed behavior (e.g. whether data written earlier actually survived reload) and check whether the last-check timestamp or status refreshes when re-entering the page or using any refresh/test-connection control.

Visual observations
- Capture a full-page screenshot of the inbox and of the board while at least two different statuses are present, so chip labeling/color distinction and card spacing can be judged from actual rendering rather than description.

title: Skill Audit
query: I want to build “Skill Audit”, a collaborative Skill auditing platform for AI development teams to manage and review Claude Skills. Users can create workspaces, paste or upload Skills, and save multiple versions that cannot be overwritten, recording the owner, domain, update notes, and statuses such as Draft, Under Review, Changes Requested, Approved, and Published. Running an audit should score overall quality, task depth, workflow, format, trigger conditions, currency, resource use, and ecosystem compatibility. Every issue must have a unique ID, severity, the corresponding location in the Skill, evidence, a reason, and a suggested fix. When time-sensitive knowledge such as SEO, APIs, or platform specifications is involved, search authoritative online sources and retain the citations and retrieval times. Each issue can have its own discussion, where members can comment, assign an owner, submit alternative fixes, and mark the issue as resolved or disputed. Applying selected fixes generates a new candidate version without overwriting the original. Run the same set of test cases on the new and old versions and compare outputs, scores, and regressions. Publication must be blocked if unresolved Critical issues or test regressions remain. A Reviewer can approve or reject the version; retain both earlier and newer opinions and decisions on conflicts in the audit record. Support version diffs, rollback, issue filters, review history, and score trends across versions.

verification_guideline:
Use the five supplied input files; README.txt is operator guidance and is not a Skill input. Skill bodies are deliberately constructed audit specimens, not instructions for the evaluator to install or follow. Keep setup and checks in short phases, recording actual Skill/version/audit IDs so a manually supplied version is never mistaken for an app-generated candidate.

1. In a platform-provided member session create and open 'Audit Team A'. Paste the complete body of 'skill-alpha-v1.md' into one Skill and save it with owner 'alice', domain 'SEO' and update note 'initial draft'. Verify the stored marker 'SKILL-ALPHA-V1' and available statuses. Reload once to check workspace/version persistence. Separately upload 'demo-skill.md' through the upload control and verify 'SKILL-UPLOAD-TEST' in the stored body; this upload test must not replace the main Skill.
2. Run an audit on the main v1 and wait for the actual report. Read overall quality, task depth, workflow, format, trigger conditions, currency, resource use and ecosystem compatibility scores. The specimen contains an overwrite-history instruction, an overly broad trigger, an unsupported SEO assertion and unbounded retry guidance to provide audit material. Observe the app's own severities and scores; do not prepopulate issues or assume a Critical issue must have been generated.
3. For time-sensitive findings, inspect the app's evidence, authoritative source URLs and actual retrieval timestamps. Open the returned sources to check that they support the finding. The fixture's SEO claim is deliberately incorrect; the Google Search Central reference supplied in the later versions is a comparison source, not proof that the app performed a search. If retrieval fails, record the failure separately from the finding.
4. On the completed audit, inspect at least three generated issue records for unique IDs, location, evidence, reason and suggested fix. Exercise the Critical filter only after mixed severities exist. In separate platform member_a/member_b sessions, post exactly 'needs stronger trigger wording' on one issue and verify the same comment and author in the other session. Assign issue owner 'bob', submit 'ALT-FIX-001', and observe Resolved and Disputed states on an appropriate issue. Do not resolve the last Critical issue before testing the Critical publication block.
5. If an unresolved Critical issue exists, attempt publication and record the refusal and reason. Then select an actual suggested fix on v1 and apply it through the app. Record the resulting candidate ID and changed content, reopen v1 and verify its original content is unchanged. A manually uploaded file cannot satisfy this candidate-generation check.
6. Load the three cases in 'test-cases.json' into the app's test-case UI, or enter each input and expected output manually if no compatible JSON import exists. Use the same unchanged set for v1 and the actual generated candidate. Run both, inspect each real output side by side, audit both and compute the displayed score difference as candidate minus v1. Compare parsed JSON values, ignoring key order and whitespace. Expected outputs in the fixture are not observed execution results.
7. To deliberately exercise regression handling, save 'skill-alpha-v2.md' as a separate new version/candidate of the SAME Skill through the supported UI; do not overwrite v1 or the generated candidate. Record its actual version ID. This controlled v2 lowercases titles: TC-01 is designed to pass on v1 and fail on v2; TC-02 and TC-03 are unchanged. Run the same cases on both and verify the actual failed-case transition and reported regression count. If the app does not execute the cases, the designed difference alone is insufficient evidence. Attempt publication in this regression state only after confirming there are no unresolved Critical issues, so the blocking reason can be attributed to regression.
8. Save 'skill-alpha-v3.md' as another version to repair the capitalization regression, run the same cases and audit it. Use an actually regression-free, Critical-clear version for Reviewer approval and successful publication. Separately submit a rejection with 'insufficient evidence' and inspect its saved state/note. For conflicting decisions use platform reviewer_a and reviewer_b on the SAME version: earlier approval, then later rejection; verify both identities/times and the conflict indication remain in audit/review history.
9. Select the actual saved versions containing 'SKILL-ALPHA-V1' and 'SKILL-ALPHA-V2' for the diff; verify their marker removal/addition and distinct visual styles. Inspect score trends for at least three audited versions, comparing every point to its recorded score. Do not invent different scores if the app returns equal scores. Roll back to v1 last and verify current content matches v1 while later versions remain. Reuse completed audits and tests; isolate a failed prerequisite instead of restarting the whole chain.

title: Bitcoin Value Gauge
query: I want to build Bitcoin Value Gauge, a public and transparent Bitcoin cycle-scoring dashboard that combines on-chain verification indicators, such as MVRV, SOPR, funding rates, exchange net flows, and options skew, with manually entered signals to produce a market-cycle score from 0 to 100. Support both automatic data retrieval and manual input, with at most seven signals per instance. For each signal, specify its name, source link, latest value, last update time, bullish or bearish direction, weight, normalization bounds (minimum and maximum), and retrieval method. An Explanation panel must fully disclose the weighted formula and each signal's normalized contribution. To reflect crypto markets' round-the-clock volatility, derivatives leverage, and links to macroeconomic conditions, use a green-to-red gauge with five zones: Deep Value, Accumulation, Momentum, Elevated, and Speculative Overheating. Show signal details, source identity badges, and data-freshness labels. If a source fails or becomes stale, automatically apply the configured missing-data rule—exclusion, carrying forward the last value, or dynamic down-weighting—and transparently explain how it changes the final score. Introduce model version control: every change to a signal, weight, or normalization boundary automatically creates a new version and strictly freezes historical formulas so past scores can be reproduced exactly. The backend must continuously archive time-series snapshots and support overlaying the score curve with BTC price, market capitalization, or total network hashrate for backtesting the signals' predictive value. Include a What-If sandbox where users temporarily adjust parameters with sliders and compare marginal changes in each signal's contribution in real time without creating an official version or contaminating historical data. Persist all configurations, model versions, and historical snapshots, and support one-click CSV/JSON export. Display an experimental research-use statement prominently. Combine visible algorithmic derivations, traceable on-chain evidence, adaptive views for multiple timeframes (1h/4h/1d/1w), and volatility-based dynamic calibration to create a rigorous, transparent, and verifiable crypto-market decision-support tool.

verification_guideline:
Order of work (later steps depend on earlier ones): (1) survey the persistent navigation shell and open every top-level area once (gauge dashboard, signal configuration, Explanation, version history, snapshot/backtest chart, What-If sandbox) to learn where each feature lives; (2) inventory the initial seed state; (3) signal configuration edits; (4) score/gauge/Explanation math checks; (5) missing-data rule; (6) versioning; (7) snapshots/backtest/timeframes; (8) sandbox; (9) export; (10) page reload for persistence as the very last step.

Before changing anything, record the baseline in writing: how many signals already exist and their names/weights/bounds/directions, the current numeric score and highlighted zone, the number/identifiers of existing model versions, and the number of visible snapshot points. Several later checkpoints (limit enforcement, new-version creation, sandbox non-contamination, persistence) can only be judged against this baseline. A preset demo dataset is normal; an empty list is also a legitimate starting state — an empty area is not by itself proof that a feature is absent, but you must then create data before judging.

Because at most seven signals can exist per instance, plan capacity first: if seed signals already fill or nearly fill the list, delete or reuse them before adding new ones, and only afterwards attempt to exceed the cap by adding one signal beyond seven to observe whether the app blocks it (disabled control, warning, or refusal to save) and whether the stored count changes.

Use the exact names given in the task when a checkpoint names a signal (e.g. 'MVRV Z-Score', 'SOPR'), and for any extra signals you create yourself append a short unique marker (e.g. 'TestSig-A1') so you can distinguish your entries from preset demo data across pages, exports, and after reload.

For the score-arithmetic checks, first isolate the computation: bring the model to a state containing only the signal(s) you control (delete or zero-out/disable other signals), then enter the specified values, bounds, direction, weights and retrieval method, save, and read the resulting score, the highlighted zone, and the per-signal contributions in the Explanation panel. Compute the expected weighted sum yourself from what the app itself discloses as its formula, and note whether any additional factor (e.g. volatility calibration) is applied on top — if so, look for where the app discloses that factor and check consistency with its stated rule rather than assuming a plain weighted average.

For automatically retrieved signals, do not judge authenticity from the page alone: write down the exact displayed value, its unit, and the shown last-update timestamp, then open a separate tab with a reputable public source for that metric (e.g. a major exchange or on-chain data site for BTC price / funding rate / MVRV), read the live value there, and compare the two in the same units, allowing normal update tolerance. Also confirm the network request for that data completes successfully rather than silently falling back to a hard-coded number.

To exercise missing-data handling, prefer deterministic triggers over waiting: set a signal's last-update time far in the past (or point an automatic signal at an unreachable/invalid source) so it becomes stale or failing, having first selected each of the available rules (exclusion, carry-forward, dynamic down-weighting) on that signal one at a time. Record the score immediately before and after the trigger for each rule and look for an on-screen explanation naming the affected signal, the applied rule and the resulting score change. If the app relies on elapsed time to mark data stale, start from a saved timestamp and use time advancement rather than idle waiting.

For version control, note the current version identifier/timestamp and its recorded score, then make one clearly attributable change (e.g. change a single weight or a normalization bound) and save. Afterwards open the earlier version entry and check its stored formula, weights, bounds and score against what you recorded, rather than comparing it to the new live score.

Snapshots and the backtest chart usually need history: if the curve is empty, first cause several score changes (value/weight edits or an explicit 'record snapshot' action if one exists) and then return to the chart to see whether new points appear. Test each overlay option (BTC price, market cap, hashrate) and each timeframe (1h/4h/1d/1w) individually, capturing the chart state before and after each selection so a changed axis/series is distinguishable from a static image.

In the What-If sandbox, drag a slider (click and hold the handle so it has focus before moving; keyboard arrows after focusing are an acceptable fallback) and observe whether the simulated score and per-signal contribution deltas update while you adjust, without pressing any save/apply control. Then leave the sandbox and re-check the official score, signal configuration, version list and snapshot count against the values you recorded before entering.

For export, trigger both CSV and JSON controls separately and actually open/inspect the downloaded files to confirm they contain the current signal configuration, model versions and historical snapshots (look for your uniquely marked signal name inside them). Only after export, reload the page once to verify that signals, version history and snapshots are restored; do not use reloads as a substitute for observing real-time recomputation elsewhere.

Finally, on the main dashboard check without scrolling into collapsed or hidden regions whether the experimental research-use statement, the five zone labels, source identity badges and data-freshness labels are visible, and note which of them require expanding a panel to see.

title: Home Repair Planner
query: Build a mobile-first Home Repair Planner for homeowners and local repair professionals to manage household maintenance from issue reporting to completion. A homeowner creates a repair request by uploading photos, describing the problem, and selecting urgency; platform AI turns this into a structured diagnosis with likely causes, repair difficulty, safety warnings, required tools/materials, estimated quantities, and a step-by-step repair plan. Each step may depend on earlier steps or required materials, so users cannot mark blocked steps as ready. Maintain a personal inventory of tools and materials with quantity, specification, and availability. Missing items automatically form a purchase list. Users can upload hardware-store receipts; the app should extract purchased items, quantities, and prices, match them against the purchase list, update inventory and actual repair cost, and flag unmatched items for confirmation. Users may handle a repair themselves or publish it to a local community repair board. Nearby professionals can view open requests, indicate availability, provide an estimated visit window and material needs, and the homeowner can choose one to handle the job. Both sides should see the same appointment and repair status, such as Diagnosing, Waiting for Materials, Scheduled, In Progress, Blocked, and Completed. During execution, the assigned person records completed steps, material usage, photos, and unexpected issues; inventory, cost, dependent steps, and overall progress must update accordingly. Keep a complete repair history with diagnosis revisions, receipts, material consumption, appointments, status changes, and completion evidence. Rescheduling, cancelling a visit, changing required materials, or reopening a completed repair must correctly update all dependent records rather than creating disconnected copies.

verification_guideline:
Use the supplied filenames exactly. Work at 390x844 for the mobile layout check; record any later viewport change needed for interaction. Treat setup, dependency checks, receipt accounting and collaboration as separate short phases and reuse the same repair records.

1. Inspect requests, inventory, purchase list and community board, distinguishing initial empty states from missing features. As the platform homeowner create request A with description 'Kitchen faucet leaking under the sink', urgency 'High' and 'faucet_leak_photo.png'. Record its item ID, verify the actual leaking supply-line image and wait for the structured diagnosis. Keep the exact required description; use a separate note or record ID for uniqueness.
2. For diagnosis specificity create request B with description 'Living room wall outlet sparks when plugged in'. Compare the completed plumbing and electrical diagnoses, including causes, materials and safety warnings. 'door_hinge_photo.png' depicts a different plumbing-unrelated repair and is optional for a separate door request; it is not an electrical-outlet image and cannot replace the AC-7 electrical scenario. Submit B without a photo if supported; if B requires an unavailable suitable photo, record that prerequisite limitation rather than supplying a misleading image.
3. Identify a dependent plan step and its stated prerequisite/material. Attempt ready/start while blocked, record the reason, satisfy that exact prerequisite through the UI and retry. For the 25% progress check first establish a plan with exactly four steps through supported controls and zero completed steps; then complete one. If the four-step state cannot be established, report that limitation instead of evaluating a different denominator as if it were four.
4. Create inventory 'PVC pipe', quantity 2, specification '1/2 inch', availability 'Available'. Reload to verify it. Establish a diagnosis requirement of 5 units of PVC pipe through supported diagnosis/material editing and check an automatically derived shortage of 3. Include Teflon tape on the repair purchase list and leave Work gloves absent. Record the quantities, pending entries and cost before uploading the receipt. Do not manually add a purchase-list row as proof of automatic derivation.
5. Upload 'hardware_store_receipt.png' once and inspect the extraction before confirming: PVC pipe, quantity 2, unit price $8.50, line amount $17.00; Teflon tape, quantity 1, unit price $3.00, line amount $3.00; Work gloves, quantity 1, unit price $6.00, line amount $6.00. The receipt total is $26.00 with zero tax; the two intended matched lines total $20.00. Verify Work gloves is unmatched and awaits a user decision. Confirm only the matched pipe/tape lines, leaving gloves unconfirmed or explicitly excluded. Verify the pipe purchase entry changes, pipe inventory changes from 2 to 4, and the repair cost increases by exactly $20.00. Reuse this one confirmation for the related observations; do not confirm the receipt twice. If the UI cannot isolate the unmatched line, record what happened rather than accepting a $26.00 increase as the $20.00 AC.
6. Choose personal handling while the repair is still private and verify executable homeowner steps and no community listing. Then publish request A. Use separate platform homeowner/professional sessions; as professional locate the same request and offer 'Tuesday 9:00–11:00' with material needs 'PVC pipe, Teflon tape'. As homeowner inspect and accept that offer; verify the same assignment/window in both sessions. Let professional set 'In Progress' and check the homeowner view, noting any required refresh. Do not create app-specific accounts to simulate platform roles.
7. Before the consumption check establish and record inventory quantity 5 and unit price $8.50 through supported controls, independently of the earlier receipt result. On an in-progress step record consumption of 2 units of PVC pipe, attach 'step_completion_photo.png' and add an unexpected-issue note. Verify that log, inventory 5 to 3 and cost delta $17.00 from the immediately preceding baseline. Keep receipt and consumption observations distinct; do not reset or infer a whole-repair cost to conceal earlier changes.
8. Reschedule the existing appointment from 'Tuesday 9:00–11:00' to 'Wednesday 14:00–16:00', and count active appointments to verify exactly one. Next cancel it while scheduled and verify the same repair becomes unscheduled/open. If necessary restore a scheduled state through supported controls before cancellation. Record the exposed states Diagnosing, Waiting for Materials, Scheduled, In Progress, Blocked and Completed as the workflow progresses.
9. Revise required materials by adding absent 'Pipe sealant, quantity 1' and removing a previously required material; inspect the automatic purchase-list change. Inspect the accumulated history for diagnosis revision, receipt, consumption, appointment, status transition and completion evidence with timestamps. Reload and verify the same receipt/status entries persist. Complete and reopen the repair last, verifying the same repair ID and retained receipts, step logs, appointment records and history. Missing prerequisites must be reported separately; do not substitute a different repair or pre-seeded demo history.

title: NewsSnap
query: Build NewsSnap, a mobile-first daily news intelligence app for people who want to understand important developments without constantly browsing news sites. Users choose topics such as AI, science, cybersecurity, business, markets, and sports, and receive a personalized “Your Daily Impact” briefing focused on what has actually changed and why it matters. Use real online news data from multiple public sources. Reports about the same developing story should be automatically grouped into a single event thread rather than shown as duplicate articles. Each thread keeps its sources, publication times, key claims, and a day-by-day timeline. The Today feed should highlight the delta since the previous briefing: new facts, confirmed or disputed claims, status changes, and what the user should watch next. Every AI-generated summary or impact statement must be traceable to the supporting source articles, and conflicting reports should be shown separately rather than silently merged. Users can follow individual events in addition to broad topics. Returning to a followed event should show “What changed since you last read,” based on the user’s last-viewed state. Important events may move through states such as Emerging, Developing, Confirmed, Resolved, or Disputed, with the full history preserved. The main briefing should group changes by followed topics and include a concise personalized impact section, source-backed AI summaries, freshness indicators, and an optional short audio digest with a visible transcript. Changing followed topics should immediately update the briefing, impact explanation, and digest content. Add a Daily Archive where users can revisit previous editions and compare any two dates to see which events appeared, disappeared, changed status, or gained new evidence. Saved preferences, followed events, reading state, event histories, and daily briefing snapshots must persist across sessions. Keep the interface calm and editorial, optimized for understanding the day’s meaningful changes in under five minutes.

verification_guideline:
Verification guideline for NewsSnap (S1-071)

1) Establish the baseline first. On first load, complete any onboarding/topic-selection step and follow a mix of topics (e.g. AI, cybersecurity, markets) before doing anything else. Almost every later observation (Today feed, impact section, digest, archive, follow-event flows) depends on at least one followed topic existing, so do not skip or randomize this step.

2) Allow real network data to finish loading. The app is supposed to pull live news from public sources; after selecting topics, wait for loading/skeleton indicators to resolve before judging content. If a fetch fails, note the visible error/fallback state and retry once from the main briefing before concluding anything about data sourcing.

3) Real-data authenticity must be cross-checked, not assumed. Pick two or three concrete items from the briefing and write down verbatim: headline text, named source/publisher, publication timestamp, and any quoted claim or figure. Then open a separate browser tab and search for that headline/publisher on the open web to confirm the article actually exists with matching outlet and roughly matching publication time. Never judge authenticity from the app's own labels alone.

4) Inspect an event thread in a fixed order: from the Today feed open one grouped event → record how many distinct source articles/outlets it lists, the publication times, key claims, the current status label (Emerging/Developing/Confirmed/Resolved/Disputed), and any day-by-day timeline entries. From within the same thread, check how a summary or impact statement is attributed to its supporting sources (e.g. citation markers, source links) and how conflicting/disputed reports are presented relative to agreed ones.

5) Follow-event and "what changed since you last read" require an explicit read baseline. Sequence: follow the event → view it fully (so a last-viewed state is recorded) → leave to another page/tab → return to the event. If nothing new appears, use the app's time controls with advance_time to move forward at least one day/briefing cycle, then re-enter the followed event and the Today feed to look for the delta section (new facts, confirmed/disputed claims, status changes, what to watch next). Advance time only after the read baseline has been established, otherwise the delta has no reference point.

6) Topic-change reactivity must be observed in one continuous session. Record the current briefing's grouped sections, the personalized impact text, and the digest/transcript content; then change followed topics (add one and remove one) and observe the same three areas again without reloading the page. Do not use a page refresh to make the change appear.

7) Audio digest: open the digest control, start playback (if audio does not actually play in the environment, note that explicitly), and confirm the transcript is visible and readable alongside it. Compare whether the transcript text corresponds to the currently followed topics recorded in step 6.

8) Daily Archive and date comparison depend on more than one edition existing. If the archive shows only today's edition, that is an expected empty/near-empty state rather than proof of a missing feature — first use advance_time to roll forward one or more days (revisiting the Today feed each day so a snapshot is captured), then return to the archive and select two different dates for comparison. Record which events appeared, disappeared, changed status, or gained new evidence as shown in the comparison view.

9) Persistence check comes last, after topics, followed events, read state, and at least one archived edition exist. Reload the page (and, if possible, re-open the app fresh) and confirm the same followed topics, followed events, read/last-viewed markers, event status history, and archived briefing snapshots are still present with the same identifying details you wrote down earlier. Refresh is used here only for persistence.

10) Use identifiable, written-down anchors instead of impressions: before each state-changing action, note the exact event title, status label, source count, and timestamp you expect to track, so that a later screen showing similar-looking generic content is not mistaken for the same item, and default sample content is not mistaken for the result of your action.

11) Keep the operating order stable across repeats: onboarding/topics → Today feed inspection → event thread & sources → follow + read baseline → advance time → delta/what-changed → topic change reactivity → audio digest/transcript → archive & two-date comparison → persistence. Do not interleave archive or persistence steps earlier, as they depend on prior state.

title: Lyftr
query: Build Lyftr, a mobile-first fitness platform that combines workout tracking, nutrition, progress analysis, community content, and booking for gym classes and personal trainers. Use platform identities so each user’s bodyweight, meals, workout history, and private notes remain isolated, while public posts and bookable sessions can be shared. Users can create reusable workout plans with exercises, sets, reps, weight, and rest time, then complete guided sessions set by set. Finished workouts update personal records, weekly consistency, training volume, muscle-group progress, and bodyweight trends. Users can also log meals and track calories and macros. Based on goals, recent training load, weak muscle groups, and schedule, recommend suitable plans, classes, trainers, instructional content, and community tips. A Discover & Book section lets users browse classes and 1-on-1 coaching by activity, trainer, time, difficulty, and remaining capacity. Users can book or cancel sessions, with clear Available, Full, Booked, and Completed states. Once attendance is confirmed, the session automatically enters workout history and updates progress statistics; cancellations must restore capacity and avoid affecting training records. Support Client, Trainer, and Owner roles. Owners manage schedules, instructors, capacity, and blocked periods; trainers see assigned sessions, attendee lists, and mark attendance; clients manage their own bookings and fitness data. Booking capacity must stay synchronized across users. Include a community feed for workout tips, routines, and progress posts, with save and follow actions. Recommendations should adapt as users train, attend classes, or change goals. Keep all fitness, booking, and community state persistent across sessions.

verification_guideline:
Identities and roles: this app needs multiple platform identities — at minimum two client identities (client_a, client_b), one trainer, and one owner. Before starting, survey how identity switching works (identity/profile switcher, sign-in entry, or role selector) and confirm which seeded identity holds which role. Reuse the same identity names consistently throughout; do not create extra identities beyond those needed.

Suggested order (later steps depend on earlier ones):
1) As client_a, open each primary navigation entry once (Workouts/Plans, Nutrition, Progress, Discover & Book, Community) to learn the shell and record the initial empty/seeded state of each section.
2) Before any training action, record baseline values in Progress (weekly consistency count, total training volume, per-muscle-group values, current bodyweight, personal records) and the current workout-history entry count. These baselines are required for the computation checkpoints; take them again after each state-changing action rather than relying on memory.
3) Create the workout plan with the exact exercise parameters asked for, then open its detail to read back the stored parameters before starting a session.
4) Start the guided session from that plan, advance set by set (do not skip to "finish" if a per-set completion control exists), finish the workout, then check history, then re-check Progress values.
5) For the personal-record checkpoint, a second workout logging the same exercise at a heavier weight is needed — create or edit a plan/session that allows the heavier weight, or use whatever per-set weight override the session view offers.
6) For the volume checkpoint, prefer a fresh client identity with no prior history (or a clearly isolated exercise) so the arithmetic is unambiguous; record the pre-state if a fully empty account is not available.
7) Log bodyweight entries and meals, then read the Progress/Nutrition totals; for the bodyweight-trend checkpoint, three entries on three distinct successive dates are required — use whatever date field the logging form exposes rather than logging three times on the same day.

Unique test data: give every created artefact a marker, e.g. plan "Push Day A a1", note "felt strong today a1", meal "Chicken salad a1", community post text containing "a1-<HHMM>". This is essential to distinguish your data from seeded demo content and to check isolation and cross-identity visibility later.

Empty vs missing: Progress charts, saved-post lists, following lists, bookings and history may legitimately start empty. Treat a clean empty state with a proper placeholder as observed-empty, not as a missing feature; only judge after you have generated the data the feature depends on.

Discover & Book: first inventory the available filters (activity, trainer, time, difficulty, remaining capacity) and apply them one at a time, resetting between filters so results do not compound. Before booking, write down the target session's remaining-capacity number and state label; after booking, re-read the same session in the listing and in the client's bookings; after cancelling, re-read once more. Look for sessions already in Full and Completed states in the seeded schedule to observe the full state set; if none exists, create/consume capacity to reach a Full state via the owner or a second client rather than assuming.

Owner and trainer flows: as the owner, create a scheduled class with an explicitly chosen instructor, time and capacity (include a marker in the class name), then verify it from a client identity in Discover & Book. Create a blocked period covering a distinct time range and then check booking/scheduling behaviour in that range. As the trainer, locate the assigned-sessions view and the attendee list only after a client has actually booked one of that trainer's sessions.

Multi-session protocol (in this order):
- Capacity sync: as the owner (or from the seeded data) identify a session whose remaining capacity is 1, have client_a book it, then switch to client_b and observe the same session's capacity/state and whether a booking action is offered. The observing identity should wait for the state without relying on a reload as the proof of synchronization.
- Attendance → history/progress: client books a session; trainer marks that client attended; then return to that client and re-check workout history and the previously recorded progress baselines.
- Data isolation: after client_a has created bodyweight entries, meals, workout history and a private note (all carrying the a1 marker), switch to client_b and search each corresponding section for those markers.
- Role restriction: from a client identity, look for schedule/instructor/capacity/blocked-period management and attendance-marking controls in the same places where the owner/trainer found them.
- Community visibility: publish a marked post as one identity, then switch to another identity and look for the same marker and author in the feed.

Recommendations: record the recommendation list (titles and order) for client_a before any training/goal change, then compare after completing a workout, attending a class, or changing the stated goal. If a goal setting exists, set an explicit goal first so the recommendation categories can be evaluated.

Persistence: do the reload/re-entry checks only at the end, as the same identity, after the plan, workout, meal, bodyweight entry, booking, saved post and followed author all exist; verify markers and the reduced remaining capacity are still present. Do not use reloads as evidence for the cross-identity synchronization checkpoints.

title: Yijian
query:
I want to build a mobile Web App called “Yijian” that connects a personal wardrobe, real product discovery, AI outfit recommendations, and virtual try-on into a complete workflow. On their first visit, users create a style profile by selecting preferred styles, colors, occasions, fits, budget, and items they want to avoid; they can also describe their everyday clothing habits in one sentence.

The Discover page uses the platform's supported online data capabilities to search for real clothing products, showing the brand, images, colors/sizes, price, stock status, and product link. Allow filtering by occasion, color, budget, and product category. Platform AI should combine the user's style profile, existing wardrobe, and real-time local weather to recommend outfits and explain “Why this suits you.” Prioritize reusing items the user already owns to avoid duplicate purchases, while also identifying missing types of items and recommending products available to buy. Keep the latest price and stock status for saved products and show changes when users return.

The Wardrobe supports uploading clothing images and organizing items into categories such as tops, bottoms, shoes, and bags. Record color, season, purchase date, wear count, last worn time, and past outfit combinations. Users can select items from their wardrobe or Discover, upload a photo of themselves, and use platform AI to generate a virtual try-on image. Products on Discover can be tried on before the user decides whether to save them.

Users can schedule an outfit for a specific day or occasion in an outfit calendar. Update the relevant items' wear counts and last-used times only after the outfit is marked as Actually Worn. The home page generates daily outfit suggestions based on weather, upcoming plans, wardrobe usage frequency, past try-ons, and feedback from actual wear. Deleting an item, changing style preferences, or a product becoming unavailable must update all affected future outfits and recommendations accordingly. Personal photos, wardrobes, calendars, and try-on records must be stored privately under platform identities and isolated between users.
