verification_guideline:
Follow this order; several checkpoints only become observable after earlier steps succeed.

1. Start from a clean first visit (fresh platform identity). Complete the style profile onboarding FIRST, before touching any other module: pick at least one style (use 'Minimalist'), one or more colors, an occasion, a fit, a budget range, an avoided item (use 'Leather'), and type a one-sentence habit description that includes a unique marker (e.g. 'daily commute look YJ073'). Save/complete, then locate where the profile is displayed afterwards (profile/settings/home) so later checks can re-read it. Do not skip onboarding by dismissing it — later recommendation checkpoints depend on a stored profile.
2. Seed the wardrobe next, since recommendations, try-on, calendar and wear-count checks all read from it. Upload the provided clothing images and create at least three items with distinct, uniquely named titles (e.g. 'White Shirt YJ073', 'Blue Jeans YJ073', 'White Sneakers YJ073'), assigning each to a different category, and fill color/season/purchase date where fields exist (use color 'white', season 'summer', purchase date '2024-05-01' for the shirt). Note the categories offered by the category selector. Open one item's detail view and record the initial wear count and last-worn value before doing anything else.
3. For the 'missing category' behaviour, you may temporarily work with a wardrobe that contains only tops (create the shoes/bags items afterwards, or use a separate stage) so that the recommendation has a genuinely absent category to detect. Plan this before adding all items if the app has no delete-and-restore convenience.
4. Real product data must not be judged from the page alone. On Discover, search a concrete keyword such as 'white shirt', then write down for one specific result its exact brand, title, displayed price, stock status and product link; open that link in a new tab (or search the brand/product externally) and compare brand, price and availability against the real source. Do the same when checking that a saved product shows refreshed price/stock. If a result link fails to resolve to a real listing, record that explicitly.
5. Apply Discover filters one at a time, resetting between them (occasion, then color, then category e.g. 'shoes', then a budget maximum of 300). After each application, record the number of results and read the relevant attribute/price of several remaining cards rather than only the first one. Also record whether each card's image visually matches its own title/brand/category.
6. Save at least one specific Discover product (note its exact title) and confirm it appears in the saved list; keep the recorded original price/stock so the later 'change indication' observation is meaningful.
7. Weather is real-world data: read the exact location, temperature and condition text shown on the home/recommendation view, then verify them against an external weather source for that same location and current time in a separate tab. Then check whether the recommendation rationale actually references that weather and the saved profile (styles, avoided items).
8. Trigger AI outfit recommendation only after profile + wardrobe exist. Wait for the generation to finish (loading indicators may take tens of seconds) before judging. To check that the rationale is not static text, generate a recommendation, then change the style profile to a clearly different style/avoided item, regenerate, and compare the two rationale texts.
9. Virtual try-on: upload the provided personal photo, select one or more wardrobe items, trigger generation and wait for the image to render; then separately start a try-on from a Discover product card and confirm afterwards that saving the product is still an available choice. Judge the resulting image by whether it depicts the uploaded person and the specific garments selected.
10. Outfit calendar: schedule an outfit on a specific future or today's date with an occasion. First observe the item wear counts while the outfit is only scheduled (not worn), then mark it as Actually Worn and re-open the same items' detail views to read the wear count and last-worn value again. Always re-read the same item you recorded in step 2 — do not compare across different items.
11. Propagation checks: after the calendar entry exists, delete one wardrobe item that is used by a future scheduled outfit (or change the style preferences), then navigate back to the calendar, home suggestion and recommendations to observe how the affected entries were updated. Navigate via the global navigation bar rather than URL guessing, and note whether all four main entries (Home, Discover, Wardrobe, Outfit Calendar) exist and open the expected views.
12. Persistence and privacy: reload the page once after the profile and wardrobe exist to check that onboarding is not re-shown and the uniquely named items/profile values remain (reload is only for persistence). Then switch to a second platform identity (fresh session/account) and inspect Home, Wardrobe, saved products, calendar and try-on records for the unique markers created by the first identity; afterwards return to the first identity and confirm its own data is still intact. An empty wardrobe/calendar/recommendation area for a brand-new identity is a legitimate empty state, not a missing feature — only report absence when the feature's entry point itself cannot be found after seeding data.

title: World Cup 2026 Odds Analysis
query: Build a football market-versus-results analysis app that compares pre-season betting-market expectations with actual competition performance. It must not include betting, payments, odds recommendations or wagering actions; it is strictly historical and analytical. Maintain competitions, seasons, teams, import batches, odds rows, result rows, saved queries and saved analyses. Cover at least four competitions of different sizes — Champions League, Premier League, La Liga and a World Cup edition — over at least two seasons each, 20 to 32 teams per competition-season. Data enters through import batches. A batch records source, capture date, competition, season and row count, and every odds row and result row belongs to exactly one batch; re-importing a competition-season creates a new batch instead of overwriting the old one. Odds rows hold decimal outright-winner odds per team; result rows hold wins, draws, losses, goals for and against, and points. A team with results but no odds, or odds but no results, is listed as unmatched, and a batch with unmatched rows or duplicate teams cannot be marked ready. Only ready batches feed the dashboard, the query library and exports. Derived values are computed, never entered by hand. Implied probability is one over decimal odds; raw implied probabilities sum to more than one, so they must be normalised within a competition-season to sum to 1.00 within a stated tolerance, with the removed overround shown. Odds rank comes from normalised probability, actual rank from points then goal difference, and rank gap from the two. Because competitions differ in team count, also compute a percentile rank gap, and the cross-competition leaderboard must use it and say so. The dashboard answers "did the market get it right?" for a chosen scope — one competition-season or several combined — showing the biggest overperformer and underperformer, the mean absolute rank gap, and a table sortable and filterable by team, competition, normalised probability, odds rank, points, goal difference, actual rank and rank gap. Editing one result row must change the metrics, ranks, leaderboards and chart together. The query library holds saved SQL queries with named parameters for competition, season and minimum matches played. A query runs against the loaded data and returns a table whose numbers agree with the dashboard for the same scope; a query referencing a batch that is not ready refuses to run and names it. Editing a query creates a new version and earlier versions stay readable. A saved analysis freezes the computed table for its scope together with the batch ids and query versions used. Later imports or query edits must not rewrite it, and two saved analyses of the same scope can be compared to show which teams moved. Export builds a pivot-style workbook view from a saved analysis, citing that analysis's batch ids and query versions rather than current data. Deleting a competition, season, team or batch still referenced by result rows, saved queries or saved analyses is refused and lists the referrers; a batch can instead be retired, hiding it from new analyses while existing saved analyses keep working. Keep raw data, queries and the summary workbook separately visible, with compact tables and a findings-first chart.

verification_guideline:
Survey before touching anything: open each top-level area in turn (raw data/catalog + batches, dashboard, query library, workbook/export) and record what is seeded — competition names, seasons per competition, team counts per competition-season, batch ids with their source/capture date/row count/ready state. Screenshot a baseline of one ready competition-season's dashboard table (team rows, normalised probability, odds rank, points, goal difference, actual rank, rank gap, percentile rank gap), the summary metrics and the chart, because later edit checks are only judgeable against this baseline.

Operation order matters. Do read-only observations first (catalog, batch row views, derived-metric arithmetic, dashboard scope switch, sorting, filtering, leaderboard), then creation steps (new import batch, saved query + edit, saved analysis), then state-changing/refusal steps (mark-ready refusals, retire a batch, delete a referenced entity) last, so that data the earlier steps depend on is not removed.

Freeze-before-change sequencing: to observe that a saved analysis is not rewritten by later activity, first save an analysis for a chosen scope and note its stored batch ids and query versions, and only afterwards perform the new import for that scope and the query edit; then reopen the earlier analysis. Save a second analysis of the same scope after the change so the two can be compared, and export the workbook from the older analysis so the cited batch ids/query versions can be checked against the newer ones.

Use unique, self-identifying test data: name new batches, saved queries and saved analyses with a short marker such as "T1432" (source label, query name, analysis title) so they cannot be confused with seeded records, and use that marker when checking lists, comparison views and export headers.

For unmatched-row and duplicate-team refusals, work inside a newly created (not-ready) batch rather than a seeded ready batch: within that batch delete or add rows so that one team has a result row without an odds row, another has odds without a result, and one team appears twice; then attempt to mark it ready and read the resulting message. Keep at least one ready batch per scope intact so the dashboard, queries and analyses still have data.

For the "only ready batches feed the dashboard/query" checks, deliberately keep one not-ready batch for a competition-season that also has a ready batch, and compare row counts/values in the dashboard for that scope against the ready batch's rows; run a saved query whose parameters point at the not-ready batch's scope to read the refusal message.

Derived-value checks require manual arithmetic from what is on screen: copy the decimal odds and displayed probabilities for a small set of teams, note the app's stated rounding/tolerance, and compute implied probability, the normalised sum, the removed overround, ranks and rank gaps yourself rather than trusting labels. For the percentile rank gap, pick two competition-seasons with clearly different team counts (e.g. a 20-team league season and the larger World Cup edition) and compare teams that share the same integer rank gap.

When testing the result-row edit, choose a team in the already-baselined scope and change its points enough to overtake the team ranked directly above it; afterwards inspect, in the same session, the dashboard table row, the mean absolute rank gap and over/underperformer summary, the chart, and the cross-competition leaderboard entry for that team, without navigating away first. Record whether each updates together.

Distinguish empty state from missing functionality: the query library, saved-analyses list, comparison view and workbook may legitimately start empty; create the prerequisite record (query, analysis) before concluding an area is absent. Likewise a not-ready batch legitimately contributes nothing to the dashboard.

Use page reload/re-entry only for the persistence-style checks (a saved analysis still showing its frozen numbers, batch ids and query versions after imports, query edits or a batch retirement); do not use reloading as a substitute for observing in-session recomputation.

If an import step requires a file, use the provided CSV fixtures; if the app instead offers an in-app import form or a simulated source selector, use that path and note which mechanism was available. Re-import the same competition-season that already has a batch so the new-batch-versus-overwrite behaviour and the per-row batch ownership can be inspected in the row views.

If the app presents its team lists, odds or final standings as genuine historical records for a named real season, first write down the specific displayed values (e.g. a champion's points total) and then compare them against an external authoritative source before making any authenticity claim; otherwise limit conclusions to internal consistency between tables, metrics, chart, queries and exports.

title: Lean Proof Assistant
query: Build Lean Proof Project Workspace, a web app for mathematicians, students, and formal-methods teams to organize Lean-style proof projects, study formal proof structure, and manage external review evidence. Use platform-provided identity and database persistence for projects, theorem drafts, proof obligations, assignments, comments, review history, and attached evidence. The workspace should include a theorem file tree, monospaced proof editor, proof-obligation panel, dependency graph, and a searchable library of definitions, lemmas, examples, and references. Users can create a theorem, split it into proof obligations, record hypotheses and dependencies, attach Lean-style code snippets or explanatory notes, and move each obligation through Draft, Needs Review, Reviewed, and Verified Externally statuses. The Verified Externally status should require reviewer-provided evidence, a verification note, or a reference to an external Lean check. In the collaboration view, the creator can assign proof obligations to up to 15 invited viewers with contributor or reviewer roles. Contributors can add formalization attempts and comments, while reviewers can approve, return, or request changes with feedback. Add learning support that explains common proof-state concepts, highlights manually annotated goals and hypotheses, and links related examples from the library. Make the UI feel like a serious technical workspace with low-saturation colors, code-focused typography, clear status chips, and a project timeline showing progress from draft to external verification.

verification_guideline:
Setup and order of work (many checkpoints build on earlier ones; follow this skeleton):
1) Sign in with the platform-provided identity as the project creator. Survey the workspace shell first (persistent navigation to proof editor/theorem workspace, collaboration, library, dependency graph, timeline) and note the overall palette and editor typography before creating data, so later screenshots do not obscure the initial layout.
2) If a project must exist before theorems can be created, create one first; an empty initial state is normal for this kind of workspace and is not by itself missing functionality.
3) Create theorem 'Riemann Lemma A', confirm it appears in the file tree, then select it so it opens in the proof editor. Only after it is open, click into the editor area (make sure it has focus) and type 'theorem two_eq : 1 + 1 = 2 := by norm_num' exactly, then save/apply if an explicit save control exists.
4) With that theorem open, create obligations in this order: 'OB-1 base case' first, then 'OB-2 inductive step' (the dependency and graph steps require both to exist). Then record the hypothesis 'h : n > 0' on OB-1, record that OB-2 depends on OB-1, and attach the Lean-style snippet or note 'by simp [Nat.succ_le]' to OB-1.
5) Status workflow on OB-1: first open the status control and record the full list of offered statuses; then move Draft → Needs Review → Reviewed one step at a time, capturing the chip after each change. Next attempt Verified Externally with all evidence/verification-note/external-check fields left empty and observe the outcome and the resulting status; only after that attempt, retry with the verification note 'Checked with Lean 4 mathlib build #221' (plus an evidence file or external check reference if the form requires one).
6) Persistence: reload the page only after the theorem code, obligation statuses, and evidence have been saved, then reopen the same project/theorem and re-check the file tree, editor content, status chip, and evidence text. Use reload only for persistence checks, never as a substitute for observing collaboration updates.
7) Cross-view continuity: after dependencies exist, open the dependency graph view and look for nodes and the connecting edge; open the timeline view after the Verified Externally transition so the corresponding entry can be looked for. Data created in the editor must be observable from these other views without re-creating it.
8) Library: open the library view, note whether definitions, lemmas, examples, and references are all represented, and pick a keyword taken from an existing entry's own title before typing it in the library search input (do not invent a keyword). For learning support, read the proof-state explanations from the theorem workspace, manually annotate a line of proof content as a goal and another as a hypothesis to observe highlighting, and activate a related-example link to see whether it opens the corresponding library entry.
9) Unique test data: append a short marker (e.g. a 3-4 character suffix or timestamp such as '-t42') to every comment, formalization attempt, and review feedback text you submit, so you can distinguish your own entries from pre-seeded sample content when checking them from another identity or after reload.

Multi-session collaboration protocol (needed for the collaboration checkpoints):
10) Use three identities at most: the creator (already signed in), viewer_a to hold the contributor role, and viewer_b to hold the reviewer role. Perform invitation and assignment as the creator first: invite the two viewers, assign 'OB-1 base case' to viewer_a as contributor and (if the app allows a second assignee, otherwise assign 'OB-2 inductive step') to viewer_b as reviewer, using each viewer's platform identity/share entry point as the app requires.
11) Then open a separate session for viewer_a (separate browser session/identity, not just a logout-login loop if the platform offers a dedicated way) and confirm what viewer_a sees as assigned, submit a formalization attempt and a comment with your unique marker, and inspect whether reviewer decision controls (approve / return / request changes) are available to a contributor-only role.
12) Then open a session for viewer_b (reviewer role) and perform all three review decisions — approve, return, and request changes — each with feedback text carrying your marker.
13) Return to the creator session and look for the contributor's attempt, the comment, and each of the three review-history entries with their feedback. For these cross-identity observations, allow the app a short wait for the state to appear rather than assuming a refresh is required; use a reload only when explicitly checking the persistence checkpoint for assignments, comments, and review history.
14) Viewer limit: invite viewers until 15 are in the invited list (reuse a systematic naming pattern for the placeholder invitees so counting is easy), then attempt a 16th invitation and observe both the response message and the resulting count in the invited-viewer list.
15) If any step is blocked (e.g. an obligation cannot be created before a theorem is saved, or an assignment control is disabled until a viewer accepts the invite), record the blocking condition and the exact screen state before moving on, instead of skipping to a later checkpoint out of order.

title: Chess Graph
query: I want to build Chess Graph, a browser-based chess opening study tool with a chessboard, an interactive repertoire graph, and controls for Import JSON, Export Backup, New Graph, side to move, and opening notes. When the user makes a legal move, the app should create or select the corresponding position node and update the graph. Clicking a node should load the matching board position, highlight the path, and allow the variation to continue. Represent branches and transpositions clearly, support White and Black repertoires, and allow annotations such as main line, sideline to avoid, and lesson focus. Include smooth pan, zoom, and drag navigation for larger graphs. Users can import a JSON repertoire and export the current graph as JSON. Repertoires, positions, notes, and layout changes should persist after refresh or re-entry for the current platform identity. Use the host-provided identity for saved data. verification_guideline:
Suggested order and stabilization notes (adapt naming to whatever the UI actually calls things):

1) Start on the main page and first take stock of the static surface: the chessboard, the graph area, and the toolbar controls (import, export, new/reset, side-to-move or White/Black repertoire selector, opening-notes field). Do this before any mutation, so the initial board setup and control inventory are recorded from a clean state.

2) The app most likely starts empty (root/starting-position node only). An empty graph, empty notes panel, or disabled annotation controls before any move is a legitimate empty state, not missing functionality — create data first, then re-judge.

3) Build data incrementally and take a screenshot after each move so node/edge changes can be compared: play 1.e4 (observe node creation), then 1...e5, then 2.Nf3, etc. Moves may be made by drag or by click-source-then-click-target; if drag does not register, retry with the click-click method before concluding the board is broken.

4) Test the illegal-move case on a freshly reset or starting position, and note the graph's node count immediately before and after the attempt so any side effect is observable.

5) Re-selection/branching/transposition checks depend on being able to click an existing node first: click the target node, confirm the board updated, then play the continuing move. For the transposition scenario, return to the starting-position node before starting the second move order, and compare the resulting node count/edges with the earlier state.

6) Annotations and notes: select a node explicitly before opening the annotation control or typing a note. Use note text that is unique and traceable, e.g. "Kings pawn plan <short marker/timestamp>", and save it explicitly if a save/apply action exists. Then click a different node and click back to confirm which node the text belongs to — this avoids mistaking sample or globally shared text for per-position storage.

7) Graph navigation (pan, zoom, node drag): make sure the graph canvas has focus/pointer over it, drag from empty canvas space for panning (not from a node), and use the wheel or the app's zoom control over the canvas. Capture before/after screenshots for each of the three interactions separately, and note the position of a reference node relative to the canvas edges so displacement and scale change can be compared.

8) Ordering constraint around reset and import/export: perform the export while the graph still contains the moves you want to see in the file; only then use New Graph to clear. Verify export content by inspecting the downloaded file (open/list it), not just by observing a toast. Use that exported file as the import source so the schema matches the app's own format.

9) The White/Black repertoire separation check should be done with a known small state (e.g. one move present under one side), then switch sides, observe, then switch back — do not refresh in between; the switch itself is what must be observed.

10) Persistence checks come last: re-create the needed state (moves, a uniquely marked note, an annotation, and a dragged node position), record what is on screen, then reload/re-enter the page and compare against the recorded state. Refresh is used only for persistence; do not use it as a substitute for observing any live update.

11) Identity: use the host-provided platform identity as-is — do not attempt to register or log in separately. If the interface surfaces the current identity, record it, and treat persistence as tied to that identity (data reappearing after reload/re-entry under the same identity).

12) If a destructive control (New Graph) shows a confirmation dialog, confirm it explicitly and verify the resulting state afterwards; note that this action removes previously created nodes, so any check still needing them must be finished first.

title: Find My Moon
query: I want a public Find My Moon web app that works immediately for casual stargazers and learners. The main view should use the user’s local calendar date to calculate an approximate lunar phase with a built-in astronomical model: estimate lunar age from a fixed reference new moon and the length of the synodic month, convert that age into the phase angle and illuminated fraction, then show the resulting phase name and illumination percentage. Present these values in a readable data panel alongside a clear illuminated Moon visual. The same calculated phase must drive an interactive 3D educational scene containing Earth, the Moon, a visible lunar orbit, and a fixed decorative star field, with the Moon’s position and lit side matching the phase shown in the panel. Let users orbit or rotate the scene by dragging or touch gestures and zoom in or out with a visible touch-friendly control or pinch interaction, while keeping the phase relationship consistent during camera movement. Include concise educational explanations of the Moon’s orbit, why the visible phases change as the Moon moves around Earth, and the limits of estimating a phase from a date rather than making an observatory-grade prediction. Clearly label the star field as decorative and explain that it does not represent the sky actually visible from the user’s location. Use the local date only, without requesting location permission or fetching a star catalog or other external astronomy data. The visual design should be dark and atmospheric, with luminous moonlight, strong contrast, readable information, and polished controls that work comfortably on desktop and touch screens.

atomic_functional_checkpoints.checkpoint: Data panel shows phase name and illumination computed from today's local date
atomic_functional_checkpoints.verification: On opening the main view without any setup, a readable data panel displays a lunar phase name and an illumination percentage that match the real lunar phase for the machine's current local calendar date (illumination within roughly ±8 percentage points and the phase name matching the true phase or an adjacent one, with no internal contradiction such as 100% labelled 'New Moon').

atomic_functional_checkpoints.checkpoint: Illuminated Moon visual matches the displayed phase
atomic_functional_checkpoints.verification: The Moon visual shown next to the data panel has a lit region whose shape and size are consistent with the panel's phase name and illumination percentage (thin crescent for a low percentage, nearly full disc for a high percentage).

atomic_functional_checkpoints.verification: Pressing and dragging the pointer (or a touch gesture) about 150 px across the 3D scene changes the camera viewpoint so the on-screen arrangement of Earth, Moon and orbit path is visibly different from before the drag.

atomic_functional_checkpoints.checkpoint: Zoom in and out changes scene scale
atomic_functional_checkpoints.verification: Using the visible touch-friendly zoom control or a pinch gesture (either is sufficient) renders the scene objects visibly larger/closer, and the opposite zoom-out action reverses the change.

atomic_functional_checkpoints.verification: The Moon's position along the visible orbit relative to Earth and the scene's light direction matches the phase named in the data panel (near the Sun-side of Earth for New Moon, opposite for Full Moon, about 90° for a Quarter phase).

atomic_functional_checkpoints.checkpoint: Moon's lit side in the 3D scene matches the phase illumination
atomic_functional_checkpoints.verification: The Moon body in the 3D scene has one hemisphere lit and one dark, with the lit side facing the scene's light source and the visible lit fraction consistent with the panel's illumination percentage.

atomic_functional_checkpoints.checkpoint: Phase relationship stays consistent during camera movement
atomic_functional_checkpoints.verification: After rotating the scene by roughly 90° by dragging and then zooming in one step, the Moon remains at the same orbital position relative to Earth and its lit hemisphere still faces the same light direction, so the phase geometry is unchanged by camera movement.

atomic_functional_checkpoints.checkpoint: Star field stays a fixed decorative backdrop
atomic_functional_checkpoints.verification: After rotating or zooming the scene, the star field remains present as a fixed backdrop behind Earth and the Moon rather than disappearing or occluding the scene bodies.

atomic_functional_checkpoints.checkpoint: Educational text covers orbit, phase change cause, and estimation limits
atomic_functional_checkpoints.verification: The educational section contains concise text on all three topics: the Moon's orbit around Earth, why the visible phases change as the Moon moves around Earth, and the fact that the phase is approximated from the calendar date rather than being an observatory-grade prediction.

atomic_functional_checkpoints.checkpoint: Star field is labelled as decorative only
atomic_functional_checkpoints.verification: A visible label or note associated with the 3D scene or explanation section states that the star field is decorative and does not represent the sky actually visible from the user's location.

atomic_functional_checkpoints.checkpoint: No location permission or external astronomy data requests
atomic_functional_checkpoints.verification: While loading the main view and interacting with the 3D scene, the app triggers no geolocation permission prompt and issues no network request to an external astronomy, star-catalog or ephemeris service, while still showing phase values derived from the local date.

atomic_functional_checkpoints.checkpoint: Dark atmospheric theme with luminous moonlight and readable contrast
atomic_functional_checkpoints.verification: The main view uses a dark background with a luminous/glowing Moon treatment, and panel text is rendered in high contrast against that background so it remains clearly readable.

atomic_functional_checkpoints.checkpoint: Usable layout and controls on a touch-sized viewport
atomic_functional_checkpoints.verification: At a 390x844 mobile viewport, the data panel, 3D scene and zoom control are all visible without horizontal overflow or overlap, and the zoom control remains large enough to be tapped comfortably.

verification_guideline:
Operation order and dependencies:
- Open the app once with no setup and let the 3D scene finish its first render before any interaction; take a baseline full-page screenshot first, since later interaction checks are compared against this initial state.
- Before touching anything, record verbatim from the data panel: the phase name, the illumination percentage, and any date the app displays. Also record the machine's current local calendar date (e.g. from the OS clock or a neutral date source). Then compare the recorded phase name and illumination against an external, independent moon-phase reference for that same local date — do not judge correctness from the app's own text, and do not assume the app is right just because its wording is internally consistent.
- Note whether the app displayed the local date it used; if it shows a different date than the machine's local date, record that discrepancy explicitly instead of silently substituting.
- Only after recording the panel values should the illuminated Moon visual, the 3D Moon position, and the 3D lit hemisphere be compared with those same recorded values; these visual checks are all relative to the panel numbers you captured.

Interaction sequence for the 3D scene:
- Do interactions one at a time and capture a screenshot immediately before and after each, so the comparison is unambiguous: (1) drag roughly 150 px horizontally across the interior of the 3D canvas (press, move in several intermediate steps, release — a single instantaneous jump may not register as a drag), (2) screenshot, (3) zoom in one step using the visible on-screen zoom control if one exists, otherwise use pinch/scroll on the canvas, (4) screenshot, (5) zoom out the same amount, (6) screenshot.
- Start the drag away from panels, buttons, text and the zoom control so the pointer press lands on the 3D scene itself and the canvas receives focus.
- For the "phase geometry stays consistent during camera movement" check, judge the Moon's position relative to Earth and the light direction within the rotated frame, not by absolute screen coordinates — the whole scene is expected to move on screen when the camera moves.
- Treat the star-field observation as part of the same post-drag / post-zoom screenshots rather than a separate manipulation.

Content and runtime checks:
- Scroll through the entire page (including any collapsed/expandable sections or tabs) to locate the educational text and the star-field disclaimer before concluding either is absent; quote the relevant sentences you find.
- Monitor for any browser geolocation permission prompt during initial load and during scene interaction; if a prompt appears, record it and dismiss it rather than granting. Also inspect outgoing network activity during load and interaction to see whether external astronomy/ephemeris/star-catalog endpoints are contacted (bundled scripts, fonts, or CDN assets are not astronomy data sources).
- Watch for console errors or a blank/black canvas that would indicate the 3D scene failed to initialize; if the scene never renders, report that instead of interpreting it as a design choice.

Responsive check:
- Perform the mobile-viewport check last, at 390x844, after all desktop observations are complete. Re-load or re-render at that size, then scroll the full page to confirm whether the data panel, 3D scene and zoom control are reachable without horizontal overflow or overlapping each other.
- Do not use browser page zoom as a substitute for the app's own scene zoom control or pinch gesture.

title: TipMap
query: Build a mobile-first Web App called “TipMap” for diners. The main screen should be an interactive map with a heatmap showing where customers tend to leave higher tips. Users can switch between average tip percentage, average tip amount, and estimated total cost per person, and filter restaurants by cuisine, price range, neighborhood, and lunch or dinner. Tapping a restaurant should open a detail card showing its typical tip range, average spending per person, estimated total cost including tip, number of user reports, and a simple confidence indicator so restaurants with limited data are not presented as equally reliable. Add a Tip Calculator where users can enter the bill amount and party size to quickly compare several tipping options and see the final total. Users can also log a dining experience by selecting a restaurant and entering the bill, tip amount, party size, and an optional note or rating. These reports should anonymously update the restaurant’s aggregated tipping statistics and heatmap, while each user’s personal dining history remains private and persists after refresh. Include a Saved & Compare page for comparing restaurants by average spending, tipping level, and estimated total cost, plus a My Dining page showing recent restaurant spending and tip totals. The overall design should feel like a modern restaurant discovery app, with a clean map interface, warm heatmap colors, and compact cards.

atomic_functional_checkpoints.checkpoint: Mobile-first compact card layout
atomic_functional_checkpoints.verification: At a 390x844 mobile viewport, the map screen and restaurant detail card render as a mobile-first layout with compact cards, no horizontal overflow, and no overlapping or clipped content.

verification_guideline:
Set the browser to a mobile viewport (about 390x844) before starting, and keep it for the whole run so the mobile-first layout and compact cards are observable.

Suggested order (later steps depend on earlier ones):
1) Land on the main map screen: confirm the persistent navigation entries, that map tiles render, and that pan/zoom respond; observe the heatmap overlay and its color palette before touching any filter.
2) Exercise the metric selector (tip percentage / tip amount / total cost per person) one at a time, recording the active metric label and any visible per-restaurant values or legend after each switch.
3) Exercise the four filter dimensions (cuisine, price range, neighborhood, lunch/dinner). Before applying a cuisine filter, first record the names/count of visible restaurants so the narrowing effect can be compared afterwards. Reset filters back to 'all' before continuing, otherwise later steps may not find the target restaurant.
4) Open a restaurant detail card by tapping a marker/hotspot. Record verbatim the restaurant name, typical tip range, average spending per person, estimated total including tip, and report count. Then open a second restaurant whose report count is clearly different, and record the same fields plus the confidence indicator wording, so the two can be compared.

Baseline capture before logging: choose one specific target restaurant and write down its exact name, report count, average tip / average spending values, and its heatmap appearance under the average-tip-percentage metric. Aggregation and heatmap-update checks are only meaningful against this recorded baseline.

Logging dining experiences:
- Use the log/report entry point (it may live on the detail card, the map screen, or the navigation bar); select the restaurant explicitly rather than relying on a pre-filled default.
- Enter the exact numeric values requested by the scenario, and always fill the optional note with a unique marker (e.g. "tipmap-test-<short timestamp>") so the entry can be distinguished from seeded sample data later in My Dining and on detail cards.
- After submitting, note whether a confirmation appears or the form closes without a remaining error, then navigate back to the same restaurant's detail card to re-read the same fields recorded in the baseline.
- For the heatmap-update check, log the unusually-high-tip report, then return to the map with the average tip percentage metric selected and compare against the recorded baseline appearance/value. Do not use a page refresh as the mechanism for this check.

Multiple logs: when a second log is required for personal totals, keep both entries' amounts and markers noted, and check My Dining only after both submissions are complete.

Persistence: perform the browser reload only for the persistence checkpoint, at the end of the single-user flow, and then re-open My Dining to look for the same uniquely-marked entry and its values.

Saved & Compare: first open Saved & Compare before saving anything to see whether an explicit empty state is shown (an empty state is not evidence of a missing feature). Then save one restaurant from its detail card, check the page, then save a second distinct restaurant and re-check so the side-by-side metrics can be observed.

Multi-session (anonymity / privacy isolation): after the reporter identity has logged an entry with the unique note marker, open a second, clean identity — a separate browser profile or incognito/private window pointing at the same app URL — and from that identity open the same restaurant's detail card and its My Dining page. Search for the reporter's unique marker and any personal attribution. Do not clear the first identity's storage; keep both sessions available for comparison. If the app has no explicit login, treat the fresh isolated browser session as the 'other user'.

Stability notes: allow the map tiles and overlay a moment to finish loading before judging the heatmap; when a value is ambiguous (e.g. a range vs a single number), record the literal on-screen text instead of paraphrasing; and if a control opens a bottom sheet or overlay, close it before navigating to another tab so subsequent taps are not blocked.

title: Movie Tracker + AI Recommendations + Shared Reviews
query: I’m a film lover and want to build an app called Screenbook where I can keep track of what I watch, get AI recommendations, and swap short reviews with invited friends. Use the current identity already provided by the host platform, with no separate sign-up or login flow. Each person’s Want to Watch and Watched lists, ratings, viewing preferences, recommendation history, and stats are private. Short reviews posted on a movie’s detail page are shared with the group, and new reviews should appear in real time for invited members viewing the same movie. The Discover page should show at least 12 popular films as portrait poster cards with the poster, title, year, and rating. Include filters for All, Action, Comedy, Sci-Fi, Romance, and Horror. At the top of Discover, add a preference box where someone can enter something like “I’m in the mood for a fast-paced sci-fi mystery.” Use the platform’s AI to return five movie suggestions, each with a one-sentence reason, and let users open the movie details from any recommendation card. Movie information can come from a movie-data service supported by the platform or from built-in sample data. The detail page should include a large poster, title, director, cast, runtime, and synopsis. Users can give a 1–5 star rating, mark the film as Want to Watch or Watched, and post a short written review. Add a Generate AI Review button that creates a relevant review of the current film and lets the user copy it. My List should switch between the user’s private Want to Watch and Watched lists and include a summary of past viewing preferences and recommendations. The Stats page should show the total number of watched films and a bar chart broken down by genre. Use a bottom tab bar for Discover, My List, and Stats. Personal lists, ratings, preferences, recommendation history, stats, and shared reviews must persist after refresh or reopening the app.

Order of operations (single identity first, then multi-identity):
1. Open the app with the host platform identity and land on the main screen; do not look for or create any account. Note the initial state of Discover, My List, and Stats before making any changes, so later changes are attributable to your own actions.
2. Do the read-only observations on Discover first (card count and card fields under the All filter, card shape/orientation, poster-to-title consistency, the filter set and the result of switching to one genre such as Sci-Fi), then return to the All filter before continuing.
3. Poster authenticity: record the exact title/year shown on a few specific cards and on one detail page, then compare each poster image with the real film's known artwork from an external source; do not judge authenticity from the page alone. Also record the displayed director/cast/runtime for at least one well-known film and check them against an external reference.
4. AI recommendations: submit the preference text exactly as given in the query, wait for the generation to finish (these calls can take many seconds; wait for a loading state to end rather than clicking again). Record the returned titles and reasons verbatim. Then submit a clearly different mood (e.g., a lighthearted romantic comedy) and record that second result set for comparison. Open a movie detail page from one recommendation card before leaving this area.
5. Detail-page actions: from a Discover card, open one film and perform in this order — set a star rating, mark Want to Watch, post a written review, generate an AI review, then use its copy control. For the copy check, paste into a text input in the app (e.g., the review box) to compare the pasted text with what was generated, then clear the box without submitting it.
6. Use unique, identifiable test content for every review you post: append a short marker such as "#a1", "#a2" plus a two- or three-digit timestamp fragment to the required review text (e.g., "Tight pacing and a great twist. #a1-742"). This distinguishes your entries from any seeded sample reviews when checking lists, cross-identity visibility, and persistence.
7. Lists and stats continuity: mark at least two different films — one as Want to Watch, another as Watched (and prefer films of different genres, recording each film's genre) — then switch to My List and confirm both sections, and to Stats to observe the total and the genre chart. Mark one additional film as Watched afterwards and re-check Stats so the count/chart change can be observed. Record exact numbers you see before and after.
8. Empty states: My List, the preference/recommendation summary, and Stats may legitimately start empty; only evaluate them after you have created the relevant data yourself. An informative empty state before data creation is not evidence of a missing feature.
9. Persistence: perform the reload only after all creation steps above are done. Reload the app (or reopen it), then revisit the rated movie's detail page, the movie with your marked review, My List (both sections and the preference/recommendation summary), and Stats, comparing against the values you recorded earlier.

Multi-session protocol (two identities, member_a and member_b):
- Use exactly two separate platform identities/sessions. Perform member_a's actions first.
- Real-time shared reviews: have both identities open the detail page of the same movie at the same time. With member_b's page left untouched (no reload, no navigation away), have member_a post a uniquely marked review (e.g., "Real-time check #ab-317") and then observe member_b's review list for that same marker to appear on its own; allow a reasonable wait for propagation. Do not reload member_b's page for this check.
- Privacy isolation: after member_a marks a movie as Want to Watch and gives it a 5-star rating, check member_b's My List and member_b's rating control on that same movie's detail page, then return to member_a to confirm member_a's own state is unchanged.
- Keep identity attribution clear: note which review markers and which list entries belong to which identity in each observation.

Stability notes:
- Click into the correct input field before typing (preference box vs. review box) and submit via the app's own submit control.
- AI calls (recommendations and AI review) may fail transiently; if an error appears, retry once and record both the error and the retry outcome.
- Before each state comparison, capture the exact on-screen values (titles, counts, star fills, review texts) rather than relying on memory of an earlier screen.

title: WorldRoute
query: Build a global trip-planning app called WorldRoute. Users should be able to search directly for any country, city, or attraction without choosing a fixed destination first—for example, Paris, Mount Fuji, the Grand Canyon, or the Louvre. Use online data sources to retrieve real information about major travel destinations and landmarks, including location, opening hours, admission prices, ratings, recommended visit length, transportation options, weather, and source links. Let users save places to a personal travel list. A user can select several cities or attractions at once, then enter a starting point, travel dates, number of days, budget, and preferences such as nature, history and culture, food, or family travel. The app should generate a multi-city or even multi-country itinerary, ordering stops around distance, opening hours, travel time, and the hours available each day, then plot the full route on a map. Each day’s plan should include attractions, transportation, estimated arrival times, visit lengths, and a daily budget. Users can drag stops into a new order, remove places, or add new ones. Any change must recalculate the transportation, timing, and budget for the rest of the trip. If a place is closed that day, the weather makes it a poor choice, or the schedule has a conflict, show a warning and suggest an alternative. Support multiple saved versions of an itinerary. For completed trips, users can add photos, actual spending, and visited status to build a personal map of their travels. Saved places, routes, versions, and past trips must persist across sessions.

verification_guideline:
Suggested execution order (later steps depend on earlier ones succeeding; if a step fails, still attempt the later ones with whatever data exists):
1. First survey the persistent navigation area and switch once through each main section (search, personal travel list, planner/itinerary, past trips) before doing anything else, so the shell and view-switching behavior are observed on a clean state.
2. Do all searching from the single free-text input: query "Japan", "Paris", "Mount Fuji", "Louvre", and "Grand Canyon" one at a time, without first picking a type/category filter. Allow several seconds for network-backed results; if results are slow or empty, retry the query once before concluding.
3. Open the detail view of Louvre (and Paris / Grand Canyon) and record verbatim the displayed identity/region, location, opening hours, admission price, rating, recommended visit length, transportation, weather condition and temperature, and the target URL behind any source link. Then open the source link or an independent external source in a separate tab and compare those recorded values against the real-world ground truth (including current Paris weather). Never judge authenticity from the app's own wording alone; note whether the source URL actually resolves to a page about that same place.
4. Save at least two places in different cities to the personal travel list (e.g., Louvre in Paris plus one non-Paris place such as Mount Fuji or Grand Canyon) — a multi-city itinerary later requires this. Verify the list view shows them, then reload the page once and re-open the list for the persistence check.
5. In the planner, select both saved places at once, then enter starting point "London", a start date, 3 days, budget 1500, and one preference (choose "history and culture" first). Generate. Record the full generated result: day sections and their dates, per-stop arrival times, visit lengths, transportation modes/durations, per-day budgets, and the trip total — you will need these numbers later to judge recalculation.
6. Immediately afterwards, regenerate with identical places/dates/days/budget but the "nature" preference and compare the two itineraries stop-by-stop. Do this before any manual editing so the comparison is not polluted.
7. For the map, verify markers/route by comparing marker placement against real geography (e.g., relative position of Paris vs. the other stop, or hover/click a marker to read its coordinates) rather than accepting any generic image; if the map fails to load, wait and retry once before recording.
8. Editing checks in this order on one generated itinerary: (a) drag the third stop of a day with three or more stops to the first position — click and hold the drag handle/stop row, move in small steps, and release only after the drop target is highlighted; if HTML5 drag does not respond, try again once with a slower press-move-release; (b) remove a stop that has a non-zero admission price; (c) use the add-place control to add "Eiffel Tower". After each edit, re-read arrival times, transportation segments, daily budget and trip total and compare with the values recorded in step 5.
9. To surface warnings, deliberately construct the triggering conditions rather than waiting for them: schedule the Louvre on its known weekly closing day (adjust the trip start date so a Louvre visit falls on that weekday), keep an outdoor stop on a day whose retrieved forecast is adverse, and pack many stops into a single day (or drag stops so travel plus visit time overruns the day) to provoke a conflict. For each warning that appears, also check whether a concrete alternative is offered and can be viewed/applied.
10. Version checks: save the current itinerary as a version, make a visible edit (remove or reorder a stop), save a second version, then open the earlier version and compare its stops/order/schedule with what was saved. Give versions unique names containing a short marker (e.g., "v1-T12", "v2-T12") so they cannot be confused with any preloaded samples.
11. Past trips: mark the trip/places as visited, upload the provided photo fixture, and enter an actual-spending amount that is a distinctive unique number (e.g., 1337). Then check the personal travel map of past trips for the visited places.
12. Persistence last: after all data exists (saved places, itinerary with route, two versions, one completed trip with photo/spending/visited), reload the page once and re-inspect each section for the same unique markers and numbers. Reloading is only for persistence checks; do not use it as a substitute for observing recalculation or warning behavior.
13. If a section is empty on first visit, treat it as an empty state and create the required data yourself before judging the feature; likewise, entries that already exist before you create anything should be treated as sample data and not counted as the result of your actions.

title: Shared Roommate Ledger + Chore Rotation
query: I share an apartment with two roommates, and we keep arguing about who owes what. Build an app called Roommate to make the day-to-day logistics easier. Use the current identity supplied by the host platform, and let the creator invite a small group of roommates without adding another registration or login flow. The ledger, chore schedule, and notice board are shared and editable by every member. New entries and changes should sync in real time for anyone online and remain available after a refresh or after reopening the app. On the Shared Ledger page, any roommate can record a group expense with an amount, category (rent, utilities, internet, household supplies, shared meal, or other), payer selected from the invited roommate list, and date. Group expenses by month. Each month should have a summary card showing the total and each person’s equal share. At the bottom, add a Settlement section that states in plain language who owes whom and how much. The Chore Rotation page should include preset chores such as cleaning the floors, washing dishes, taking out the trash, and buying household supplies. Show them in a weekly grid with chores as rows and the seven days as columns; each cell displays the roommate responsible that day. A cell can be edited manually, or users can tap Auto-Rotate to cycle assignments among the three roommates. Tapping a completed chore turns the cell green and adds a check mark. On the Notice Board, roommates can post text updates such as “Friends are coming over next Friday—let’s tidy up beforehand.” Sort posts newest first. Posts marked Important stay at the top and use a red border. Use a bottom tab bar for the three pages.

verification_guideline:
verification_guideline:
- Start as the creator identity supplied by the host platform. Do not look for or expect a signup/login screen; simply open the app and note where the current user's name/identity is displayed. If the app opens directly into one of the three pages, that is the intended entry point.
- Complete membership setup first: use the invite/roommate management entry to add exactly two roommates before doing anything else. Give them clearly distinguishable names (e.g. "RmB_82" and "RmC_82"). Almost every later checkpoint (payer options, per-person share, settlement, chore grid names, auto-rotate) depends on the group having three members, so re-verify the member list shows the creator plus the two invited roommates before continuing.
- Expect an empty initial state on the Shared Ledger and Notice Board. An empty list with a visible composer/add-entry control is not evidence of a missing feature; create data yourself before judging list, grouping, sorting, or summary behavior.
- Suggested minimal operation order: (1) confirm bottom tab bar and switch through all three tabs once; (2) invite the two roommates; (3) add ledger entries; (4) inspect month grouping, monthly summary card and settlement text; (5) go to Chore Rotation for manual edit, Auto-Rotate and completion toggle; (6) go to Notice Board for posting, ordering and Important styling; (7) do persistence reloads; (8) do the multi-session real-time checks.
- Ledger data plan: add at least one expense dated in January 2025 and one dated in February 2025 so month grouping can be observed, and add two separate January 2025 expenses so the monthly total and per-person share can be read from the January summary card. Keep the payer of the January expenses fixed to a single member so the settlement wording is unambiguous. Before opening the category selector, record every category option offered; before opening the payer selector, record every payer option offered, and compare the payer options with the current member list.
- Use unique, identifiable test content so results cannot be confused with any preloaded sample data: e.g. notice texts "Note One 82a", "Note Two 82b", an Important post "Important X 82c" followed by a normal post "Later Y 82d", and the required long text about Friday guests. Record the exact string you typed and search for that exact string when checking ordering, persistence, and cross-identity visibility.
- Chore Rotation: first read the grid structure (which axis holds chores and which holds the seven days) and record the assignee currently shown in a few reference cells (note the row/column by name, not by pixel). For the manual edit, change one specific cell (washing dishes / Monday) and record the before and after names. Take a full-grid observation immediately before and immediately after tapping Auto-Rotate so the whole row-by-row assignment pattern can be compared; do not judge Auto-Rotate from a single cell.
- Completion state: tapping a cell may either open an edit control or toggle completion. Determine which interaction the app uses (e.g. tap vs. long-press vs. a checkbox/marker inside the cell) before concluding, and describe the visual difference between the toggled cell and a neighboring untouched cell.
- Persistence checks: only after the ledger entry, the manually edited chore cell, and at least one notice post exist, reload the app (and, if available, close and reopen it), then return to each of the three tabs and look for the same unique markers. Persistence must be verified per page, since data is created on different tabs.
- Multi-session collaboration protocol (use exactly two identities: the creator and one invited roommate):
  * Open the invited roommate in a separate session/identity and confirm it lands in the same shared group without any registration or login step.
  * Ledger sync: keep the roommate session sitting on the Shared Ledger page, then have the creator add an expense with a unique amount/description (e.g. 150, utilities, dated 2025-01-12). Observe the roommate's already-open page and wait for the entry to appear on its own; do not reload, re-navigate, or switch tabs in the observing session for this check.
  * Chore sync: keep the creator session on the Chore Rotation page, then have the roommate change one clearly identifiable cell's assignee. Observe the creator's already-open grid for the change without refreshing.
  * Notice sync: keep the creator session on the Notice Board, then have the roommate post a uniquely worded notice (e.g. "Trash day moved to Thursday 82e"). Observe the creator's already-open board without refreshing.
  * If nothing appears after a reasonable wait, record that observation as-is; a refresh may only be used afterwards to distinguish "not synced live" from "not saved at all", and must be reported as a separate follow-up, never as evidence of real-time sync.
- Record concrete on-screen values (totals, per-person share, settlement sentences, assignee names, post order) as text in your notes before moving on, so later comparisons do not rely on memory of earlier screenshots.

title: StateMachine Studio: State Machine Designer and Validator
query: Build a responsive web app called StateMachine Studio for product managers and developers to design, validate, and simulate finite-state machines. The project list should support creating, duplicating, archiving, searching, and importing JSON projects. Use a zoomable canvas where users can add, drag, and connect states; designate exactly one initial state, any number of regular states, and multiple final states; and define each transition with an event, priority, action description, and optional guard. Guards may use only structured fields, comparison operators, and AND/OR groups. Never execute JavaScript or other arbitrary code. Validation should catch missing or duplicate initial states, unreachable states, non-final states with no outgoing transitions, missing final states, invalid fields, duplicate transitions, and cycles. Show every issue both in an issue list and on the corresponding canvas node. The simulator begins at the initial state and processes input fields, events, guards, and priorities one step at a time. For every step, show the guard result, source state, target state, and action. If no event matches, remain in the current state and add the attempt to the run timeline. Users can branch a simulation in two, compare final states, paths, and step counts, and find the shortest structural path from the initial state to a selected state. Creators can save versions, compare changes to states and transitions, restore an earlier version, and export the model and validation report. Restoring must create a new version rather than overwrite history. Invited viewers may run simulations, comment on a specific state or transition, and submit Approve or Request Changes, but they cannot edit or publish. Publishing must be blocked while critical validation errors or unresolved change requests remain. Persist projects, canvas data, validation results, simulation runs, versions, and comments. Include a fixed order-approval fixture with an unreachable state, duplicate transition, invalid guard, cycle, and event sequences with expected outcomes.

verification_guideline:
Preparation and ordering
- Open the app and first record the entry view: whether a project list with pre-seeded projects (including the built-in order-approval fixture) or an explicit empty state is shown. An empty list with a proper empty-state message is not by itself a missing feature.
- Keep two working contexts separate: (a) the built-in order-approval fixture project, used for validation, simulation, and shortest-path observations because it is meant to already contain defects and defined event sequences; (b) a scratch project you create yourself, used for destructive edits (removing/duplicating initial states, deleting final flags, adding isolated states). Never perform destructive edits on the fixture project before you have finished the validation/simulation observations you need from it.
- Use unique, identifiable test data: project names, state names, event names and especially comment text should carry a short marker (e.g. 'chk-1423') so you can distinguish your artifacts from seeded sample data.

Project list sequence
- Perform project-list checks in this order: create 'Order Flow A' → duplicate it → create a second project named 'Payment Flow' → use the search field with 'Order' → clear the search → archive 'Order Flow A' and then look for it via an archived filter/tab/label. Archiving before searching will invalidate the search observation.
- For import, use the provided JSON fixture. The import control may accept a file picker or a paste-JSON textarea; if only pasting is supported, open the fixture file, copy its text and paste it. After importing, open the created project and inspect its canvas for the imported states/transitions.

Designer / canvas
- Open a project from the list to reach the designer before attempting any canvas checks. For zoom, use the explicit zoom affordance (buttons/slider/fit) if present; capture a screenshot before and after so the scale change is comparable.
- For adding, dragging and connecting: click the node body to give it focus first, then press-hold, move in several small increments, and release; note the node's on-screen position before and after. For connecting, use the app's dedicated connect handle/mode rather than a plain drag if both exist.
- After marking initial/final states, re-check the whole canvas (not just the last node touched) to see how many nodes carry each role marker.

Transitions and guards
- Open a transition's editor via selecting the edge (or an edge list/inspector) and enumerate the available fields before typing anything. Then save concrete values (e.g. event 'submit', priority 1, action 'notify reviewer', plus a guard) and reopen the editor/edge to see what was persisted.
- Build a guard with at least two conditions combined into an AND/OR group, save it, then reopen it to check that the structure is redisplayed as built. Separately, look for any free-form code/expression input, and try entering text such as alert(1) as a comparison value to observe how it is stored and shown.

Validation
- Run validation on the fixture project first and record the full issue list (type + affected state/transition), then look at the canvas to see whether the same items are flagged on nodes/edges.
- For defect types the fixture does not already contain, reproduce them one at a time in the scratch project (no initial state; two initial states; a state with no incoming edge; a non-final state with no outgoing edge; no final state at all; a transition with empty event or incomplete guard; two identical transitions; an A→B→A loop), re-running validation after each change and undoing it before creating the next one, so results are not confounded.

Simulator
- Start a fresh run and record the current state before sending any event. Advance strictly one step at a time and read the newest timeline entry each time.
- To observe guard behaviour, send the same event twice with input field values that should and should not satisfy the guard. For priority, use a source state that has two transitions on the same event. For the no-match case, send an event that is not defined on the current state.
- Branch only from an in-progress run (after at least one step), then advance each branch with a different event before opening the comparison view. Use the shortest-path feature by selecting a target state and compare the returned path against the edges visible on the canvas.

Versions, export, roles, persistence
- Version flow order: save version 1 → add one state and one transition → save version 2 → compare the two versions → restore version 1 → then re-open the version history to see how the history changed after restoring.
- Trigger export and record what is actually produced (download entry, preview panel, or copied text) rather than assuming.
- For viewer-side behaviour, use the app's role/identity switcher or invite flow (a second browser session only if the app really supports separate identities); act as creator first, then as viewer. As viewer, run a simulation, leave a comment attached to a specific state and one attached to a specific transition using your unique marker, and submit Approve or Request Changes; then return to the creator context to attempt publishing while validation errors and/or unresolved change requests exist, and check whether editing/publishing controls are available to the viewer.

title: AI Memory Graph
query: Build a dark, technology-inspired web app for industry research and structured learning. The main workspace has two columns: an AI conversation on the left and a knowledge-graph canvas on the right. A user can enter a topic such as “Map out the main branches of machine learning algorithms.” Use the platform’s AI to produce a clearly structured response and turn its key points into nodes under the current topic. The right-hand canvas should use a dark grid background and glowing connections to link topics, branches, and source cards. Clicking a node opens its summary, key concepts, source notes, and related conversations. Show the current topic at the top—for example, Machine Learning Algorithms—and include a Current Branch view that focuses on one learning path. Add an Import from Excel node or button. After a spreadsheet is uploaded, parse it into structured entries, create field cards from the column headers, and add them to the graph. Details such as name, category, and notes should be available from each node. Support panning by dragging, expanding and collapsing nodes, a zoom slider at the bottom, plus and minus controls, and a percentage readout. Keep conversations, imported data, and node relationships synchronized with the page state. The visual style should stay dark and card-based, with restrained neon highlights and smooth animated connectors, so the research process feels like building a knowledge map that can keep growing.

verification_guideline:
Execution order and stabilization notes for this app:

1. Baseline first: open the app and, before typing anything, record the initial state of both columns (existing conversation messages, any pre-seeded nodes and their labels, the zoom percentage readout). Later you must be able to tell newly created content apart from demo/seed data. An empty conversation or a canvas holding only a root/topic placeholder is a legitimate empty state, not a missing feature.

2. Drive everything from the left conversation panel: type the exact topic "Map out the main branches of machine learning algorithms." into the conversation input and submit it. Wait until the AI reply has finished rendering (text may stream in; watch for a loading/typing indicator to disappear) before judging anything about the answer or about new nodes. If an error or quota message appears, capture it verbatim instead of retrying blindly.

3. Node generation depends on step 2: only after the reply is complete should you inspect the right canvas for nodes derived from that answer and their attachment to the current topic node, and only then check the topic title shown at the top of the workspace.

4. For the AI-authenticity checkpoint, submit a clearly different second topic in the same conversation (for example "Outline the main stages of semiconductor manufacturing."), wait for it to finish, and record distinctive wording from both answers so the two can be compared for topic relevance and non-placeholder variation. Note whether each answer has real structure (headings, numbered/bulleted points).

5. Node detail view: click a generated branch node with a single, stationary click (a click that moves may be interpreted as a canvas drag). Note which sections the opened detail view exposes and where they appear (side panel, drawer, modal). Do the Current Branch / focused-path view only after a branch node has been selected, and record what the canvas shows before and after switching into that view.

6. Excel import: locate the import affordance (a dedicated node on the canvas or a button in the toolbar/conversation area), activate it, and upload the provided fixture spreadsheet. If the file chooser rejects one format, retry with the alternate fixture file. After upload, first check the parsed structured entries (preview/list of rows), then check the canvas for field cards named after the column headers and their connection into the existing graph, then click the node corresponding to the row "Gradient Boosting" to inspect its detail values. The fixture rows are deliberately distinctive—verify the values shown match the uploaded rows rather than generic sample data.

7. Canvas controls: perform them one at a time with a screenshot before and after each. For panning, press on empty canvas background (not on a node or connector), drag roughly 200 px in one direction, and compare node positions. For collapse/expand, first identify the control on a parent node (it may only appear on hover or selection). For zoom, record the percentage readout before and after each of: dragging the slider toward its maximum, clicking minus, clicking plus.

8. For animated connectors and the dark grid/glow styling, take two screenshots a couple of seconds apart with no interaction in between so any drawing/flowing/pulsing motion can be compared; do not interact while capturing.

9. Persistence is the last step only: after the topic(s) have been answered and the spreadsheet imported, reload the page once and re-inspect the conversation thread, the imported field-card nodes, and their connections to the topic node. Do not use reloads earlier as a substitute for observing live state updates.

10. If any action opens a new view, panel, or tab, return to the main workspace before starting the next checkpoint so the canvas and conversation stay in a comparable state.

title: ColorWalk v3
query: Build a mobile web app called ColorWalk for friends who take walks together and photograph the colors they find along the way. Give it a fresh, relaxed look with green as the main color, rounded cards, and a Polaroid-collage feel. verification_guideline:
Suggested execution order (later steps depend on earlier ones succeeding):

1. First survey the app before changing anything: open the home page, note whether the shared album already contains seeded photos or is empty, and record (a) the exact number of photo cards in the feed, (b) the distinct uploader names visible, and (c) the participant avatars shown at the top. An empty or near-empty initial album is a legitimate starting state, not a missing feature — in that case create the data yourself via the upload flow before judging the Life Board or map pages.

2. Establish platform identity first. If the app offers sign-in / member selection / an invite or shared-album entry point, complete it before uploading, so that uploads can be attributed to a known identity. Record which identity you are acting as.

3. Uploads must be traceable. Use the provided fixture images and, whenever the upload flow allows a caption/title/note or location field, type a unique marker such as "MEMA-<HHMM>" (identity initials + short timestamp). Never rely on default sample content to prove that an upload worked — always look for your own marker afterwards.

4. Baseline-then-change discipline for the linked views. Before adding any new photo, visit the Life Board (activating its generate control) and the Color Trail page, and write down the summary line numbers, the map points and their per-point photo counts. Only after these baselines are recorded should you upload one more photo from the home page and revisit both pages to compare. Do this in the order: home feed → Life Board → Color Trail → upload → Life Board → Color Trail.

5. For location-related behaviour, upload at least two photos whose location resolves to the same place and at least one at a clearly different place, so grouping and per-point counts can be observed. If the app does not read location from the image file, use whatever manual location/place picker the upload flow offers and choose the same place twice, then a different place; record which place you assigned to each photo.

6. Map authenticity must not be judged from the page alone. Pan and zoom the map, then read concrete on-map evidence (street names, place labels, district/city names, or coordinates the app displays) and compare those readings against an independent external source (e.g., a public map service opened in another tab) to confirm the geography is real and that markers sit at the locations you assigned. Also confirm the map reacts to pan/zoom instead of behaving like a fixed picture.

7. Marker-style control: exercise each of the three style options in turn from the control at the bottom of the Color Trail page, taking a screenshot after each selection, and observe whether the change happens in place without reloading the page. Do not reload between style switches.

8. Life Board numbers: after generating the board, read the date, the full summary line, and cross-check each number against what you counted yourself in the feed (photo count, distinct uploaders). To probe whether the distance value is data-driven rather than fixed, note it before and after adding a photo at a new location.

9. Cross-page continuity: any photo you add on the home page must be looked for again on the Life Board and the Color Trail page within the same session; navigate between pages using the app's own persistent navigation rather than typing URLs.

10. Multi-session protocol (for the shared-album synchronization check only): use exactly two identities, member_a and member_b, in two separate browser sessions/contexts. Have member_a upload a photo carrying its unique marker while member_b already has the shared album feed open; member_b should wait and observe without refreshing to see whether the new item and its uploader attribution appear. Only if nothing appears after a reasonable wait may member_b reload, and in that case explicitly note in your report that the item appeared only after a manual reload.

11. If an upload dialog requires a file picker, use the provided fixture files; if the app instead simulates a camera capture with built-in stock images, still identify the newly created card by its position/timestamp/caption and note that the app did not accept a real file.

12. Take a screenshot after each state-changing action (before/after upload, before/after each marker style change, Life Board generation) so that counts and visual details can be compared later.
