title: Polar Night Expedition
query: Build a turn-based mobile survival game called Polar Night Expedition. The player leads a research team deep into the Arctic and must cross several camps, reach the final research station within a limited number of days, and return with enough scientific samples. Each turn represents one day. The player chooses an action—press onward, rest in place, search for supplies, repair equipment, or take a detour around a dangerous area—then spends stamina, food, and fuel as time advances. Keep the team’s health, body temperature, morale, food, fuel, medicine, equipment durability, and current location visible at all times. Weather changes daily, and random events can include blizzards, extreme cold, ice cracks, equipment failures, injuries, or discovered supply caches. Give the player several ways to respond; each choice should affect resources and the route ahead, and some events can be handled safely only with the right equipment or supplies. The map should contain several plausible routes. Shorter routes carry more risk, while safer routes take longer and consume more resources. To win, the team must reach the final station before the deadline with at least one healthy member and the required number of samples. The run ends in failure if every team member becomes incapacitated, food or fuel runs out with no way to resupply, or the deadline passes. At the end of each run, show survivors, remaining resources, samples collected, time taken, and a log of key events, with an option to start over.

verification_guideline:
- Set the browser window to a 390x844 mobile viewport BEFORE starting any run, and keep it there for the whole verification so layout observations and gameplay observations come from the same session. Only change the viewport if a later step genuinely requires it, and note the change explicitly.
- Complete any intro/setup screen first (difficulty, team naming, route choice, etc.). If a route must be chosen before the first day, record the full route list first: for each route note its name, stated length/estimated days, and stated risk wording, then pick one deliberately so later location changes can be attributed to that route.
- Before every action click, record the visible status values (day counter, location, health/stamina, temperature, morale, food, fuel, medicine, equipment durability, samples collected vs. required, weather). Take one screenshot before and one after each action, and only read post-action values AFTER dismissing/resolving any event popup or day-result panel, so the panel does not hide the updated HUD.
- Advance days one at a time and keep a written day-by-day table (day number, action chosen, weather, event name, option chosen, resulting value deltas). This single log supports the turn/day-increment, weather-variation, event, and end-of-run summary observations without needing to re-play days.
- Exercise each of the five daily actions at least once, choosing the moment appropriately: use 'rest' only after stamina/health has already dropped below its starting value, and use 'repair' only after equipment durability is below maximum (advance a few days first, or trigger an equipment-failure event). Use 'detour' at a point where the game indicates a hazard/dangerous segment ahead; if the option is unavailable at the current camp, keep advancing and retry rather than concluding immediately.
- For event handling, when an event appears, record its title, all offered options, any option shown as disabled/locked with its stated requirement, and the post-choice deltas. When the same event type reappears later (in the same or a later run), deliberately pick a different option so the two outcomes can be compared.
- To observe requirement-gated resolutions, first deliberately drive the relevant resource to zero or the equipment to broken (e.g., repeatedly choose options that spend medicine, or skip repairs until durability bottoms out), then continue advancing until an event needing that resource appears, and record whether the safe option is offered, disabled, or resolves differently.
- Plan multiple runs and use the start-over option from the summary screen between them; note the exact starting-state values of run 1 so a later fresh run can be compared against them. A reasonable plan: Run A = shortest/riskiest route played to its conclusion; Run B = longest/safest route, recording days elapsed and cumulative food/fuel spent at an equivalent progress point for comparison with Run A; further runs to reach the remaining endings.
- Deliberately steer runs toward each ending rather than relying on chance: for the victory ending, prioritize 'press onward' plus sample collection and reaching the final station before the stated deadline; for the deadline ending, repeatedly rest/search until the day limit passes; for the resource-exhaustion ending, avoid searching and keep pressing onward until food or fuel hits zero; for the all-incapacitated ending, repeatedly choose the riskiest event responses and skip healing. If an ending cannot be reached within a reasonable number of days, record how many days were played and what the game showed instead.
- When each run ends, capture the final in-game HUD values on the last playable screen (or the last logged day) BEFORE the summary appears where possible, then compare the summary's survivors, remaining resources, samples, days taken, and event log against your day-by-day table, checking that logged events appear in the order they actually occurred.
- For event-type coverage, rely on accumulated sampling across all runs plus any in-game codex/help/journal or route-briefing text that enumerates hazard types; do not treat a short single run as sufficient sampling, and state clearly how many days/events were sampled.
- The game is turn-based, so no real-time waiting should be needed; if an animation or transition delays the HUD update, wait for it to settle before reading values instead of clicking again, and never count a day twice because of an unresolved event popup.

title: PaperPulse
query: Build an academic research tracker called PaperPulse that pulls the latest papers and research updates each day from public sources such as arXiv, OpenReview, and Semantic Scholar. Users can follow areas including large language models, agents, RAG, multimodal systems, and reinforcement learning, as well as create their own alerts for keywords, authors, institutions, and conferences. Refresh results automatically each day and organize them by research area, paper type, and source. Detect and merge multiple versions of the same paper, duplicate listings across sites, and minor title changes instead of showing separate records. Each paper card should include the title, authors, affiliations, publication date, abstract, source link, and time of the latest version. Based on the abstract, use the platform’s AI to write a one-sentence contribution summary, highlight the main method, and explain why the paper relates to the user’s interests, while always retaining the original source. Users can save papers, mark them Read or To Read, add notes, and follow particular authors or topics. Organize the home page into New Today, Trending, Updates from Followed Authors, and For You. When an existing paper gains a new version, code repository, conference decision, or author update, add the change to that paper’s timeline instead of creating a duplicate. Support combined filters for date, keyword, author, institution, conference, and source, and let users save filter sets. Store a daily snapshot so users can compare what was added, updated, or removed between any two days. Saved papers, reading status, follows, notes, and historical snapshots must persist across sessions.

verification_guideline:
Suggested execution order (many checkpoints depend on earlier state being created; follow this skeleton to avoid re-work):
1) First survey the app without changing state: locate the persistent global navigation and confirm which entries lead to the home feed, saved library, filters/alerts area, and the daily snapshot comparison view. Visit each top-level view once so later steps know where controls live.
2) On the home feed, exercise the section/tab switching (New Today, Trending, Updates from Followed Authors, For You) and any grouping/organizing controls (research area, paper type, source) before creating personal data, so the baseline lists are known.
3) Then perform the state-creating actions in this order: follow research areas (at least 'RAG' and 'reinforcement learning', plus check that large language models, agents, and multimodal systems are offered), follow one named author taken from a specific paper card (write down that author's exact name), create a keyword alert (e.g., 'retrieval-augmented generation') and a second keyword alert for 'diffusion', configure and save a filter set, save a paper, set its reading status, and add a note.
4) Only after those follows/alerts exist, re-check the personalized sections (For You, Updates from Followed Authors, alert results, relevance explanations) — these are expected to be empty or generic before any follow exists, and an empty state at that point is not evidence of a missing feature.
5) Do the persistence check last: reload the page (or reopen the app) once and re-inspect the saved paper, reading status, note, followed area, followed author, saved filter set, and stored snapshots.

Stability and evidence notes:
- Use unique, identifiable test content for anything you create: e.g., note text like 'note-test-<HHMM>', an alert or saved-filter name like 'set-<HHMM>'. This prevents mistaking pre-seeded demo data for the result of your own action.
- Before following an author or applying filters, copy the exact author/institution/conference/source strings from an actual paper card so the filter or follow can plausibly match existing data; inventing values may yield an empty result that is ambiguous.
- For combined filtering, apply the criteria one at a time and record the result count after each addition, then read every remaining row to check it satisfies all applied criteria. Also confirm the panel exposes all six dimensions (date, keyword, author, institution, conference, source) even if you only combine two or three.
- For deduplication/version-merging checkpoints, do not rely on a single card. Scan or search the full feed for the same (or near-identical) title to confirm whether one or several cards exist, and open the card's detail view to inspect its source badges, version list, and latest-version timestamp.
- For the timeline: open the detail view of a paper that visibly has update activity (look for badges such as new version, code, or decision). Record the event types and the full ordered list of dates before judging ordering. If the app offers any way to simulate ingesting a new update (a refresh/fetch/simulate-day control), trigger it and then re-count how many cards exist for that paper.
- If the app exposes a manual 'refresh/fetch today' or day-advance control for the daily cycle and snapshots, use it to generate at least two distinct snapshot dates before attempting the two-day comparison; if only long-running timers exist, use advance_time and only after the refresh cycle has actually started. Do not assume snapshots exist until you have opened the snapshot list.
- Real-data authenticity: pick one displayed paper and write down its exact title, author list, publication/latest-version date, and stated source as shown on the page; then open its source link (and/or search that title on arXiv, OpenReview, or Semantic Scholar in a separate tab) and compare the values against that external record. Also note which distinct sources appear across the feed. Do not judge authenticity from the page's own labels alone; if a link fails to resolve or opens a generic search page, record that exact outcome.
- AI-generated fields (contribution summary, main method, relevance explanation) must be judged against the same card's original abstract, so expand the card and read the full abstract text and the source link/attribution in the same screenshot context before evaluating the AI text.
- Keep a written record of counts and titles at each step (e.g., number of cards before/after a filter, number of alert entries before/after creation) since several checkpoints depend on before/after comparison rather than a single screenshot.
- If a control requires typing (note, alert keyword, filter set name), click into the field first to give it focus, then submit with the explicit save/confirm control rather than assuming auto-save; afterwards re-open the item to confirm the stored value.

title: LinguaPath
query: Build a comprehensive language-learning web app called LinguaPath, with support for widely studied languages such as English, Japanese, Korean, French, Spanish, and German. After a learner chooses a target language, current level, and daily goal, create a learning path that combines vocabulary, grammar, reading, listening, and situational practice. Track study streaks and progress through each stage. Add a separate Course Explorer where users can search for topics such as the Japanese te-form, the French past tense, or Korean honorifics. Use online search to find relevant public tutorials and preserve their sources, then use AI to organize the material into leveled lessons with explanations, examples, common mistakes, and practice exercises. Completed grammar topics should automatically enter Grammar Review, where learners can search by topic and see their mastery level. Users can also import an article or choose an authentic news story, tap unfamiliar words for definitions, and add them to a personal vocabulary list. Schedule vocabulary and grammar reviews dynamically based on accuracy, response time, repeated mistakes, and how recently an item was studied. Incorrect answers should move into targeted practice. If a learner edits past study records, recalculate mastery and the upcoming plan. Keep course progress, vocabulary, and weak areas separate for each language, restoring the correct state whenever the learner switches languages. The home page should show today’s tasks, current streak, progress in each language, and a weekly AI learning report.

verification_guideline:
Recommended execution order and stabilization notes for LinguaPath (do not skip the setup step; most later modules depend on it):

1) Bootstrap first: complete the initial learning setup before touching any other module. Choose Japanese as the target language, a Beginner level, and an explicitly non-default daily goal (e.g. 20 minutes / a specific item count). Write down the exact values you chose — later home-dashboard and today's-task observations must be compared against them.
2) Establish the baseline path state: after setup, open the learning path view and record (a) the total number of stages, (b) the stage types listed, and (c) the exact progress indicator value (percentage or x/y) BEFORE completing anything. Then complete stages one at a time, re-reading the progress indicator after each completion. Prefer completing a grammar-type stage early, since the Grammar Review module depends on a grammar topic having been completed somewhere first.
3) Empty states are expected at the start: Grammar Review, personal vocabulary, weak areas / targeted practice, study history and the weekly report may legitimately be empty until you generate activity. Always produce the prerequisite data yourself before concluding a feature is absent; note in your reasoning which action was supposed to populate the view.
4) Course Explorer: search a concrete topic (e.g. "Japanese te-form", then "Korean honorifics" or "French past tense"). Wait for any AI/search generation to finish (loading spinners, streaming text) rather than judging a half-rendered view. Open at least one generated lesson and scroll through the whole lesson body before assessing its sections; also run one practice exercise end-to-end (submit an answer, and separately submit a deliberately wrong answer).
5) Real-world data authenticity (Course Explorer sources and authentic news): first copy the exact source titles, site names and URLs shown on the page, and the exact news headline/publisher/date shown in the reader. Then verify them against an external ground-truth source — open the cited URL in a separate tab or search the headline online — and compare wording, publisher and date. Do not judge authenticity from the app's own rendering, and treat clearly fabricated/unreachable links or headlines absent from the real web as such.
6) Reading & vocabulary: for the import path, paste a short article whose text contains a unique marker (e.g. a sentence including "LP088-marker") so you can tell imported content from bundled samples. After the article renders, click a single specific word, note that exact word and the definition shown, then use the add-to-vocabulary action and check the personal vocabulary list for that same word.
7) Review scheduling requires deliberate, asymmetric input: in a review session pick two identifiable items, answer item A correctly and quickly, and answer item B incorrectly after an obviously longer pause. Record both item names and any displayed next-review date/interval/queue position immediately afterwards. For the repeated-mistake check, run a second session and miss the same item B again; if a second session is gated by a cooldown or a next-day schedule, start the gate first and then use advance_time to move past it rather than waiting idly.
8) Weak areas / targeted practice: the item you answered incorrectly is the one to look for by name — search the targeted practice view for that exact item rather than accepting any generic list.
9) Study-record editing: before editing, note the record's current value, the related item's mastery level in Grammar Review or the vocabulary view, and its next scheduled review. Then change one past record (e.g. incorrect → correct, or the duration), save, and re-read the same three places to compare against your recorded baseline.
10) Multi-language isolation: only after Japanese has distinctive data (a uniquely named saved word plus at least one completed stage) set up a second language (French) through the same setup flow. Switch the active language to French and inspect course progress, vocabulary and weak areas; then switch back to Japanese and re-inspect. Do this by using the in-app language switcher, not by reloading; use a page refresh only when you additionally want to test persistence.
11) Home dashboard last: after the study activities above, return to home and read today's tasks, the streak value, the per-language progress indicators and the weekly report. To exercise the streak, complete every task listed for today and re-read the streak/day marker. For the weekly report, note whether it names your actual studied items/accuracy/weak areas from this session and whether it is (re)generated on demand or is fixed text; if generation is asynchronous, allow it to finish before judging.
12) Throughout, use unique, traceable test content (custom vocabulary word, marked article text, chosen topic names) and record exact on-screen values before and after each state-changing action, so that comparisons are based on observed numbers rather than impressions.

title: LabWizard
query: Build a collaborative lab knowledge and experience platform called LabWizard. Researchers can upload manuals and SOPs in PDF, JPG, or PNG format. Extract searchable text while preserving references to the original file, page, and paragraph, so a query such as “AFM probe calibration” can jump directly to the relevant page. Users can leave practical annotations on a specific page or step, reply to discussions, or post experimental questions. Likes, bookmarks, and follows should help recommend similar manuals and experience posts. Using multiple documents in the workspace, the platform’s AI can draft a candidate SOP with citations, a quick-start mind map, and step summaries, but it must never overwrite the source material. An administrator must review a candidate SOP before it can become the recommended version. Keep version history for each manual, provide a diff view, and allow one version to be marked as recommended. While running an experiment, users can check off SOP steps and record parameters and anomalies. Link each anomaly back to the step where it occurred so it can be found later. New material or discussion updates may produce a new candidate version, but previous review decisions and execution records must remain intact.

verification_guideline:
Use the six supplied documents by exact filename. The three PDFs have native selectable text; the JPG/PNG pages are raster-only and require actual OCR. Values are synthetic evaluation examples. Reuse uploaded documents, candidates and run IDs across short checks; do not recreate the whole workflow for each AC.

1. In the platform researcher_a session inspect the document workspace, discussion/Q&A and experiment execution navigation. Upload 'afm_manual.pdf', 'probe_storage_scan.jpg' and 'sop_page_scan.png' separately, verifying all three formats and filenames in the document list. Then upload 'probe_maintenance_sop.pdf' for a second related source and 'seed_germination_manual.pdf' for a different topic. Hold back 'sop_page_scan_update.png' until the regeneration/version phase. Pasting text or opening demo data is not proof that a required upload succeeded.
2. In 'afm_manual.pdf', verify extracted text and source filename/page/paragraph identifiers. Search exactly 'AFM probe calibration': the relevant heading and paragraph 2.3.1 are on page 2, with marker 'AFM-CAL-P2-A731'. Record the search-hit locator and click it to verify the same file/page/passage opens. Inspect the JPG's distinct 'STORAGE-JPG-6N8Q' content and the PNG's 'SOP07-REVA-4L2K' content to distinguish actual OCR results from reused PDF text.
3. Add 'Check probe tip wear' on manual page 2. On that page have researcher_a add 'Calibrate before every run'; in a separate platform researcher_b session verify the same annotation and author. Record annotation IDs/times rather than replacing required phrases. Reply 'Same issue on our tool' in the intended thread and post exactly 'Why does my AFM image drift?' once in Q&A. Record initial and final like counts, bookmark/follow lists and controls.
4. For topic-sensitive recommendations record a baseline, engage with the AFM manual and inspect the resulting recommendations. Then engage with the seed-germination document and compare the recommended topics/items. The seed document uses tray, sprout and leaf terminology and is intentionally unrelated to probe calibration. If related experience posts must be created to make the comparison observable, create clearly attributed posts in the supported Q&A UI; a lack of seeded recommendations alone is not proof of a missing update. Record the actual recommendation result rather than assuming the files force it.
5. Establish a previously approved recommended SOP version first, using an existing identified approved version or by drafting a baseline from 'afm_manual.pdf' and 'probe_maintenance_sop.pdf' and having the platform administrator approve it. Record its version ID and source contents. Then create the next pending candidate from those two explicitly selected documents. Inspect ordered steps, step summaries and a topic-specific hierarchical mind map. Check citations against the selected filenames and real pages/paragraphs, including the maintenance source's distinct content; source documents and the earlier recommended marker must remain unchanged.
6. For the source-contrast check make a separate draft from 'seed_germination_manual.pdf' and inspect its filenames, terminology and source locators. Do not attach this unrelated draft to the AFM version chain. A candidate merely displaying citation-shaped text does not establish that it used its selected source.
7. With the AFM candidate still pending, use non-admin researcher_b to check that approval/recommendation controls are unavailable or rejected. In the separate platform administrator session approve that same candidate. Return to researcher_a, reload as permitted by the AC and verify the candidate is now approved/recommended. Keep baseline and candidate review decisions with their identities/times. Do not treat the absence of an app-specific login switch as proof that platform sessions cannot be used.
8. On the approved SOP add 'Wait 30s before scan' specifically to step 3. Start a run, check off step 1, record 'Scan rate = 1.2 Hz', and while step 3 is active record 'Tip crashed during approach'. Inspect the completed count and step link; leave/reopen and follow the anomaly link. Reload to confirm all three saved values and the same run ID persist.
9. Now add 'sop_page_scan_update.png' as revised material through the SAME manual/SOP's version or new-material workflow. Rev A has 0.4 Nm and 0.5 V; Rev B has 0.6 Nm and 0.8 V plus 'Re-verify calibration after thermal settling'. Verify creation of a new pending candidate without replacing the approved recommendation. A second unrelated document entry alone does not establish a new version. Compare the selected old/new versions for their actual text additions/deletions and visual distinction; inspect full version history and timestamps.
10. Recheck earlier review decisions and the existing run's step completion, parameter and anomaly after regeneration. Test switching the recommended marker through the authorized role only after observing that an unreviewed candidate cannot replace it. Preserve earlier records when checking the new marker and default opened version. If extraction, generation, approval or session setup fails, report the specific unreachable checks and available evidence; do not fabricate a source locator, approval or cross-session result.

title: Smart Bookshelf + Book Search + Reading Check-Ins
query: A few friends and I run an online book club and want to build an app called Bookworm Circle. Use the current user identity supplied by the host platform and allow up to 15 invited members, with no separate account flow. Persist records for books, personal shelf entries, reading check-ins, progress corrections, reviews, ratings, likes, group reads, and group-read members so everything remains after a refresh. Keep books separate from personal shelves. Whether a book is entered manually or found through keyword search, first create one canonical book record with its title, author, cover, and total page count. Each person’s shelf entry points to that record, so several members adding the same book still share one canonical entry. Reject deletion of any book record still referenced by a shelf entry or review, and list the references that block it. Shelf entries have Want to Read, Reading, or Read status and can be filtered by status. Reading progress must be calculated from check-in records, not stored as an editable number. If progress needs correcting, create a correction record, recalculate the total, and keep the correction history. A book without a total page count cannot be checked in, and any check-in that would push cumulative pages beyond the total must be rejected. Each day, a member can choose a book from their Reading shelf and log pages read. A check-in updates that book’s progress, the monthly page total, and the reading calendar at the same time; calculate all three from check-in records rather than separate counters. When cumulative pages reach the total, automatically mark the shelf entry Read; users cannot set that status directly. Reviews may be written only for completed books and include a title, body, and 1–5 star rating. The community page groups reviews by book and shows a review count and average rating calculated live from individual reviews. Calculate like totals from like records, and allow each member to like a given review only once; reject duplicate likes. New reviews and likes should appear for other online members without a refresh. Keep each member’s shelf, progress, check-ins, and corrections private and exclude them from every other member’s views and statistics. Only reviews, ratings, and likes are shared in the community area. For a group read, a member chooses a book, sets start and end dates and a page goal, and invites others. Show each participant’s completion percentage, calculated from that person’s check-ins for the book during the event, without exposing the underlying check-in details. At the end, create an immutable results snapshot with everyone’s final completion status. Later check-ins must not change it, and past snapshots remain viewable. Use bottom navigation for Shelf, Check-In, Community, and Group Reads.

verification_guideline:
verification_guideline:
- Expect an empty-data app on first load: there is no seeded catalog, shelf, review, or group read. Almost every checkpoint depends on data you create yourself, so an empty Shelf/Community/Group Reads list at the start is a legitimate empty state, not a missing feature. Build the data in the order below and only then judge behaviour.
- Establish the baseline first: open the app (it should land straight in a functional view under the host-supplied identity), touch each bottom-navigation entry once (Shelf, Check-In, Community, Group Reads) to confirm the sections and their empty states, then return to Shelf.
- Core data chain (do not reorder): (1) manually create the canonical book 'Deep Work' / 'Cal Newport' / 300 pages with a cover; (2) add it to the shelf with status 'Reading'; (3) go to Check-In and log 60 pages, then log 30 more; (4) inspect progress on the shelf/check-in view, the monthly page total, and the reading calendar; (5) create a progress correction taking cumulative pages to 120; (6) only afterwards attempt the over-limit check-in test. Steps 4–6 are meaningless if step 3 did not actually create records — always confirm the check-in record appears in a list/history before continuing.
- Additional books you will need, created early so later steps are not blocked: a short book with a total of 100 pages added as 'Reading' (used to reach 100 cumulative pages and observe automatic status change, and later to enable review writing), a second book left with no total page count (or 0/blank if the form allows it) for the no-page-count check-in attempt, and at least one book kept in 'Want to Read' so the status filter has something to hide.
- For the over-total rejection, first drive 'Deep Work' cumulative pages to 280 using ordinary check-ins/corrections, verify the displayed cumulative value, and only then submit a check-in of 40 pages; afterwards re-read the cumulative value to see whether any record was created.
- If the app enforces one check-in per book per day (a second same-day attempt is blocked or merged), use advance_time to move the clock forward one day between check-ins instead of concluding the feature is broken; advance time only after the first check-in has been recorded. Note in your report whenever you had to advance time.
- Use unique, identifiable test content: review titles/bodies, group-read names, and correction notes should carry a short marker (e.g. 'Great Focus Guide A1-1432' or a member tag plus 2–3 digits). Later, when checking persistence, cross-identity visibility, and snapshots, search for that exact marker so pre-existing demo content is never mistaken for your result.
- Reviews depend on completion: try to open the review/write-review entry for a book that is still 'Reading' before you complete any book, note what happens, then finish the 100-page book through check-ins so its shelf entry becomes 'Read', and write the marked review with a star rating from there. For the average-rating observation you need two reviews with different star values on the same book (the second one from the other identity).
- Attempt book deletion only after the book is referenced (shelf entry and/or review exist), and read the resulting message and the catalog list carefully to see whether the record survives and which references are named.
- Persistence: perform reloads only after each data group is created (books, shelf entries, check-ins, corrections, reviews/likes, group-read snapshots) and confirm the same marked items and the same derived numbers reappear. Reloading may not be used as a substitute for real-time observations.
- Multi-session protocol (two identities are enough: member A = initiator, member B = second member; open them as separate sessions/profiles of the same app):
  * Canonical-record sharing: after A has 'Deep Work' on their shelf, have B add the same book (via search or the same title/author) and compare whether both point to one catalog record rather than two entries.
  * Privacy isolation: with A's shelf entries, check-ins, corrections, calendar and monthly totals in place, inspect B's Shelf, Check-In, calendar and statistics views for any trace of A's data, and confirm what B does see in Community.
  * Live updates: place both A and B on the Community tab viewing the same book; then have A submit the marked review and, separately, click like on a review. B must simply wait on the already-open view for the new review and the incremented like count to appear — do not refresh, re-navigate, or switch tabs on B while waiting; only if nothing appears after a reasonable wait should the observation be recorded as such.
  * Duplicate like: have A like the same review a second time (re-click / re-open and click again) and record the resulting count and any message.
  * Group read: A creates the event choosing a book both members can read, setting start and end dates and a page goal, and inviting B; then both members log check-ins for that book inside the event window, and you compare each participant's displayed completion percentage against the pages each logged versus the goal. Afterwards end/close the event to produce the results snapshot, log one more check-in for the same book, and re-open the snapshot to see whether its values moved; reload once and re-open past snapshots.
  * Member limit: to probe the 15-member cap, use whatever invite mechanism exists (member picker, invite list, repeated invites) and record the message and resulting member count when going beyond the limit; if the platform exposes fewer than 15 selectable identities, state that the cap could not be driven to its boundary instead of inventing a verdict.
- Cover images: if the book form accepts an uploaded image, use the supplied fixture; if it only accepts a URL or auto-fetches a cover from search, use that path instead and simply record which cover is shown, checking that it is a real rendered image consistent with the book rather than a broken/placeholder graphic.

title: Weekly Family Meal Planner + Grocery List + Nutrition Dashboard
query: I plan meals for a household of three every week and want to build a Family Meal Planner. Persist records for recipes, recipe versions, ingredients, recipe ingredient lines (ingredient, quantity, and unit), weekly plans, meal slots, grocery items, recognition drafts, and weekly reports. Everything should remain after a refresh. Include at least 20 starter recipes. Each recipe needs a cuisine (Chinese, Western, Japanese, or light meals), difficulty, cooking time, calories, separately stored ingredient lines, and step-by-step instructions. Run cuisine filters, calorie sorting, and name searches on the server. Editing a recipe creates a new version without overwriting the old one. Reject deletion of a recipe referenced by any weekly plan or favorite, and list the references that block it. Favorites must persist. The weekly planner is a seven-day by three-meal grid. Each slot can use a saved recipe or a manually entered dish; manual dishes must also be stored and completed with ingredient details. Two meal slots can be swapped. A swap leaves the week’s total ingredients unchanged while exchanging the calorie totals for the two days. Build the grocery list by aggregating ingredient lines from the exact recipe versions used in the current week. Combine matching names and units, and group items under Produce, Meat, Seafood, Seasonings, Staples, and Other. Use only ingredient details already stored in the database; flag inconsistent units or missing quantities for confirmation. Each item can be checked off as purchased. Calculate purchased and remaining counts live from the item records rather than keeping separate counters. Calculate daily totals, weekly totals, and daily averages for the nutrition dashboard from the current meal slots and compare them with a reference target of 2,000 calories per day. Any change to a meal slot must update both the grocery list and the nutrition dashboard. A Dinner Inspiration feature picks a random recipe from the library and can be narrowed by difficulty and available time: under 30 minutes, under one hour, or any length. Users can draw again, then add the chosen recipe to a specific meal slot, triggering all downstream updates. For photo recognition, let the user upload a picture of a dish and estimate its name, calories, ingredients, and method. Save the result as an editable draft. Only add it to the recipe library after the user confirms it, retaining the original image and recognition result as sources. Unconfirmed drafts must not appear in the recipe library, weekly plan, or statistics. Once confirmed, the recipe can be assigned to meal slots and included in the grocery list and nutrition dashboard. Do not generate a weekly nutrition report while any ingredient is still awaiting confirmation. The report should use stored meal slots and ingredient lines, preserve a snapshot of the plan it was based on, and give specific suggestions for the following week, such as which food group to add or which meal to replace. Users can apply suggestions to next week’s plan with one tap, updating its meal slots, grocery list, and nutrition dashboard together. The current week’s report and snapshot remain unchanged and available for comparison.

verification_guideline:
Use the two dish images in separate recognition runs, selecting the exact filename each time. Other test data is created through the app UI. Run short checks in controlled phases and record actual recipe/version/slot IDs; do not combine all mutations into one unverified end-to-end result.

1. Visit Recipe Library, Weekly Planner, Grocery List, Nutrition Dashboard, Dinner Inspiration, Photo Recognition and Weekly Report. Before editing starter data verify at least 20 distinct recipes and inspect cuisine, difficulty, time, calories, ingredient lines and ordered steps. Test Japanese filtering, calorie ordering and a name substring search, clearing filters afterwards. For backend filtering/sorting/search inspect actual request parameters and the response driving the list; a changed list or spinner alone is insufficient evidence.
2. Establish the swap state first: assign distinct recipes A and B only to Monday dinner and Thursday dinner, leaving the other slots on BOTH days empty. Record their different calories, both daily totals, weekly total and aggregated grocery lines. Swap Monday dinner and Thursday dinner; verify names exchange, the two daily totals exchange, and grocery names/units/quantities and weekly total remain unchanged. The empty-other-slots precondition is necessary for the AC's full daily-total exchange expectation. Do this before the later Monday 400/600/500 kcal setup.
3. In Tuesday lunch enter 'Tomato Egg Noodles' with at least one explicit ingredient/quantity/unit line and save. Keep a saved recipe in Monday dinner and reload to verify both required slots. Mark that Monday recipe as a favorite, verify favorite persistence and attempt deletion while the plan and favorite references both exist; inspect the rejection and named Monday-dinner/favorite references.
4. Establish recipe R version 1 with '200 g chicken' through supported recipe controls before assigning it to two current-week slots. Verify automatic grocery contribution and a single chicken/g line totaling 400 g, accounting separately for any other existing chicken contribution. Edit R to create a newer version with '500 g chicken' and calorie value 777. Check earlier/current versions, reload and verify both persist. title: PawLife
query: Build a pet growth and health app called PawLife for keeping a lifelong record of cats and dogs, from their early months through old age. Users can create profiles for multiple pets with breed, birthday, sex, spay or neuter status, weight, allergies, and other details, plus a profile picture and growth photos. Keep each pet’s data separate. Based on species, breed, age, and region, use online data sources to provide reliable guidance on diet, exercise, training, vaccination, parasite prevention, and common health risks. When a pet reaches a new life stage, update the care advice and upcoming plan on the home page while preserving earlier stage records. Users can regularly log weight, food, exercise, bowel habits, and growth photos and view trends over time. In the health section, allow uploads of examination reports, lab results, prescriptions, and similar documents. Use AI to extract test results, diagnoses, medications, and follow-up dates into a medical timeline. AI should organize records and explain general information only; it must not replace a veterinarian’s diagnosis. Users can create schedules for vaccines, parasite treatments, and veterinarian-prescribed medication and record what was actually completed. Delays or edits should update future reminders without overwriting history. Support shared family care, synchronizing feeding, walks, medication, and appointment status. The home page should bring together today’s tasks, recent health changes, and a growth report.

verification_guideline:
Operate in the order below; later checks depend on data created earlier, so do not skip the setup steps.

1. Setup first (the app likely starts empty): create the primary pet 'Mochi_<mark>' (cat, British Shorthair, birthday 2023-05-01, female, spayed/neutered = yes, weight 4.2 kg, allergies 'chicken'), where <mark> is a short unique marker (e.g. initials + 2-digit time) so you can always tell your data from any bundled sample data. Then create a second pet 'Rocky_<mark>' (dog, 18 kg) only when you are ready to test per-pet data separation. If the form offers a region/location field, fill it during creation; otherwise locate it later in profile editing or settings. An empty list before you create anything is a legitimate empty state, not a missing feature.
2. Attach the profile picture and at least one dated growth photo to the primary pet right after creation, using the provided image fixtures; note where the app expects them (profile edit vs. daily log vs. gallery) and check the resulting avatar/gallery in the pet's own detail view.
3. Per-pet isolation: add at least one weight log to the primary pet only, then switch the active pet to the second one, observe what is shown, and switch back. Do this by using the app's pet switcher, not by reloading.
4. Reload/persistence checks (profiles, logs, uploads) should be done once after the corresponding data has been created; a reload is acceptable only for persistence, never as a substitute for observing live cross-user updates.
5. Daily logs and trends: record weight, food, exercise, bowel habit, and a growth photo for the primary pet, embedding <mark> in free-text fields. For the trend chart you need at least three weight entries on three different dates — first try backdating the log date in the form; if the app only accepts 'today', use advance_time to move the clock forward between entries and log again. Record the exact values and dates you entered so you can compare them with what the chart plots.
6. Care guidance & life stage: open the guidance view for the primary pet and note which topics are present. Then create/edit pets to compare guidance across profiles — a young dog (e.g. Labrador Retriever with a birthday ~3 months before today) versus an older cat (~10 years old) — and capture the diet/exercise/vaccination text for each. Next, change one pet's region to a clearly different country/climate zone and re-open guidance to see whether parasite/vaccination content changes. Finally, edit the young dog's birthday to ~4 years before today and return to the home page to observe the life stage, care advice, upcoming plan, and whether earlier-stage records/history are still reachable.
7. Real-world data authenticity: for the guidance module, first copy the concrete text/values shown on the page (core vaccine names, intervals, parasite-prevention recommendation, region) and check whether opening guidance produces an outbound network request that returns data (observe network/loading behaviour). Then compare the recorded values against an authoritative external veterinary reference (e.g. WSAVA/AAHA vaccination guidelines or an official animal-health site opened in a separate tab). Do not judge authenticity from the page's own wording alone.
8. Health records & AI extraction: in the Health section, upload the provided report image fixtures for the primary pet, one dated earlier and one dated later. Before uploading, note the exact test result, diagnosis, medication name, and follow-up date printed in each fixture. After upload, record what the app displays as extracted fields and compare them field-by-field with the fixture content; also observe whether an actual AI/model request is issued and completes (loading indicator plus a network call), rather than instant fixed text. Then check the medical timeline ordering of the two records and look for the AI non-diagnostic disclaimer anywhere in the health area or on a record.
9. Schedules & reminders: create schedules for a vaccine ('Rabies Booster_<mark>' with an explicit due date), a parasite treatment set to repeat monthly, and a vet-prescribed medication. Mark the parasite treatment as completed with an actual completion date 5 days after its scheduled date (use the app's date field, or advance_time if the app only accepts 'now'), then read and write down the next generated due date and the original scheduled date. Afterwards edit the future schedule date once and re-check whether the earlier completion entry with its original scheduled/actual dates is still listed.
10. Home dashboard last: after schedules and logs exist, return to the home page and check that today's tasks, recent health changes, and growth report are aggregated there. Create or adjust one schedule item so it is due today, confirm it appears in today's tasks, mark it completed (from home or schedule view) and observe the home page state without reloading.
11. Multi-session family sharing (two identities: 'owner' and 'family_member'): as 'owner', open the shared family care entry for the primary pet and create the invite/share result (code, link, or member entry). Open a second independent session as 'family_member' and join/accept using that share result. Then, with both sessions open, have 'owner' change feeding, walk, medication, and appointment task statuses (use the <mark> in any task text) and observe the 'family_member' session waiting for the update to appear on its own — do not refresh or re-navigate the family member's session to force the update. Only if the app has no real-time channel at all should you note what you observed instead.
12. General stability: keep the active pet explicitly selected before every module check, because most views are pet-scoped; if a module appears empty, first confirm which pet is active before concluding a feature is absent.

title: FitLog
query: Build a fitness-tracking app called FitLog for everyday workout logging, progress tracking, and consistent routines. Support running, cycling, walking, swimming, strength training, yoga, jump rope, and sports. Store the measurements relevant to each activity, including start time, duration, distance, pace, average and maximum heart rate, and calories burned. Strength workouts should also record exercises, sets, reps, and weight. Users can start a live workout or add a past session manually. When a record is edited or deleted, recalculate weekly and monthly statistics and goal completion. The home page should show today’s activity, current streak, workout count this week, total duration, distance, and calories, plus a calendar showing the activity type and completion status for each day. Users can set weekly targets for workout count, total time, running distance, or calories. Build a weekly training plan from those goals and recent activity. Mark a planned workout complete automatically when it is finished. Missed sessions can be moved to another date, but completed history must never be overwritten. Add a workout library with video lessons grouped into fat loss, strength, mobility, yoga, and running. Each lesson includes difficulty, length, target area, and exercise steps. Users can save a lesson or add it to their training plan, and completing a guided workout should create the matching activity record automatically. The profile page should show the share of each activity type, heart-rate and calorie trends, longest streak, and a monthly summary. Workout history, goals, plans, and completion states must persist across sessions.

verification_guideline:
General preparation
- First survey the app: locate the persistent global navigation (Home, Workout Library, Profile, and any Goals/Plan entries) and note where workout history, goal settings, and the training plan live. Do this before creating data, so later steps do not get lost.
- The app may start empty or with seeded demo data. Record what already exists (existing workouts for this week/month, existing goals, existing plan items) before adding anything, and compute expected totals relative to that baseline rather than assuming a clean slate. A correct empty state is not the same as a missing feature.
- Use distinguishable test data so new records can never be confused with seeded samples: give each manually added session a recognizable combination (e.g., a distinctive note/title marker or an unusual distance/calorie value), and keep a written log of every record you create (type, date, start time, duration, distance, HR, calories).

Recommended operation order (later steps depend on earlier ones)
1. Inspect the workout creation/logging entry point and enumerate all selectable activity types before submitting anything.
2. Add one or two manual past/today sessions with full measurements (start time, duration, distance, average and max heart rate, calories) so detail-view, pace, home summary, calendar, and profile statistics can all be observed afterwards.
3. Add a Strength training session with at least one named exercise including sets, reps, and weight; then open its detail view.
4. Run the live-workout flow once (start, observe the timer, finish/save) and then confirm the resulting record in history.
5. Set weekly goals (workout count, total time, running distance, calories) before generating the weekly training plan, since plan generation is expected to derive from goals.
6. Generate the weekly plan, then exercise plan-related behaviors (auto-completion, rescheduling a missed session, regenerating the plan).
7. Explore the Workout Library (categories, lesson detail, save, add-to-plan, guided completion).
8. Check the Profile/statistics page last, after enough varied records exist (at least two different activity types and several days).
9. Do a page reload at the very end for persistence checks.

Date and time handling
- Many checkpoints depend on specific dates (today, yesterday, tomorrow, a past date). Read the app's own notion of today from the calendar/home before choosing dates, and always set the date field explicitly in manual forms rather than relying on defaults.
- For streak observation, create workouts on consecutive days (today and yesterday) and deliberately leave the day before empty.
- If the manual form separates date and start time, fill both; if only a datetime picker exists, set both parts.

Live workout and timers
- For the live session, let the timer visibly advance by taking at least two observations spaced apart; if the app requires a long duration or has a countdown/rest timer, use advance_time only after the timer has actually started, and prefer short increments so the elapsed value stays plausible.
- Guided lesson workouts may also involve a timer or a step-by-step player; drive it to its completion state (finish/complete action) rather than closing it early, then look for the auto-created activity record in history.

Edit / delete recalculation
- Before editing or deleting, record the current weekly and monthly totals and goal progress values exactly as displayed. Perform exactly one change (e.g., change only the distance of one session, or delete one session), then re-read the same indicators on the same pages. Only compare like with like.
- Keep at least the minimum records the later checkpoints need; do not delete records you still need for profile statistics or persistence.

Plan-specific cautions
- For auto-completion, ensure the planned item and the workout you log share the same activity type and the same date; do not manually toggle a completion checkbox first, otherwise the automatic behavior cannot be observed.
- For rescheduling, pick an uncompleted planned item on a past date and move it to tomorrow; afterwards check both the original date and the new date.
- Before regenerating the plan for the "completed history" check, note the exact completed item(s) and their underlying activity records; after regeneration, re-check the same date cells and the workout history.

Cross-page continuity
- Data created in the logging flow or the library (saved lesson, planned lesson, guided-completion record) must be verified on the corresponding destination page (Home, Plan, Profile, history). Always navigate to that page rather than judging from a toast/confirmation message.

Persistence
- Only at the end, reload the page (or reopen the app) once and re-visit history, goals, and the training plan to confirm the same entries, targets, and completed/uncompleted states, using the unique markers recorded earlier.

Other
- For lesson thumbnails/video previews, judge semantic consistency with the lesson title and category; if a video element exists but cannot play in the environment, note the presence and playability controls instead of forcing playback.
- If a required control seems absent, search alternative entry points (overflow menus, long-press/right-click, detail pages, settings) before concluding it is missing, and state clearly which entry points were checked.

title: StepMath
query: Build an app called StepMath for students who want to learn how problems are solved, not just see the answer. On the home page, students can type a math problem or take or upload a photo. Use the platform’s vision tools to recognize the question and turn it into a clean mathematical expression, then ask the student to confirm it before solving. Support common topics including algebra, equations, functions, geometry, probability, and introductory calculus. The heart of the app is interactive, step-by-step instruction. Do not reveal the entire solution at once. Break each problem into stages, explain the goal of the current step, and ask the student to enter a result or choose the next operation. Continue after a correct response. When an answer is wrong, point out the specific issue and offer options such as Give Me a Hint, Why Does This Work?, and Explain It More Simply. Students can open the standard solution at any time and ask follow-up questions about individual steps. At the end, show the full derivation, final answer, and concepts used. Add a More Practice feature that uses AI to create two or three questions on the same concept at different difficulty levels, then adjusts the next question based on the student’s performance. Incorrect problems should automatically go into a Review Notebook with the original question, mistaken step, correct solution, and related concepts. Support searching and filtering by problem type. A Learning History page should summarize problems completed, accuracy, frequently missed concepts, and recent progress. Persist every problem, solution path, and review record after refresh. Use a clean white background, blue and purple accents, and clear formula cards. The experience should feel like a patient private tutor guiding the student’s reasoning one step at a time, not an answer lookup tool.

verification_guideline:
Suggested execution order (later checks depend on earlier ones succeeding; do not skip ahead):

1. Start on the home page with a fresh/empty app state. Before creating any data, open the Review Notebook and the Learning History entries once from the global navigation to record their initial (possibly empty) appearance — an explicit empty state at this stage is normal and must not be treated as a missing feature; re-check them only after data has been generated.
2. Primary anchor problem: on the home page type exactly '2x + 5 = 13' into the math-problem text field and submit. If an interpreted-expression / confirmation screen appears, note it and only then confirm to enter the guided session. Do all step-level checks (AC-9 through AC-19) inside this one session; scroll the whole solving view each time so you can tell what is currently revealed versus hidden.
3. Inside the session, deliberately perform the WRONG answer first (e.g. submit '2x = 18' or another clearly incorrect result) before submitting any correct step result. This single wrong response is what unlocks the specific-issue feedback, the three help options ('Give Me a Hint', 'Why Does This Work?', 'Explain It More Simply'), and the automatic Review Notebook record. Trigger each of the three help options one at a time from the same step and capture each returned text separately so they can be compared with the original step explanation.
4. Still on the first/current step (before finishing), exercise the 'view standard solution' control and the per-step follow-up question control (e.g. ask 'Why do we subtract 5 from both sides?'). If opening the standard solution closes or ends the guided session, note that and continue the session afterwards.
5. Then answer the remaining steps correctly until the session completes, and record the completion view (full derivation, final answer, concepts). Only after the session is complete, activate More Practice: wait for AI generation to finish (do not judge on a half-streamed response), write down each generated question together with its stated difficulty label, then answer one practice question INCORRECTLY and record the difficulty of the question offered next; if the flow allows, answer another one CORRECTLY and record that next difficulty too.
6. Photo input: use the take/upload-photo entry on the home page and upload the provided fixture image. Wait for the recognition/processing indicator to settle, then record the exact expression the app extracted and compare it with the text visible in the image. If a webcam-capture-only dialog appears, prefer the file-upload path.
7. Topic coverage: from the home page, submit and confirm one short problem for each of algebra, equations, functions, geometry, probability, and introductory calculus (e.g. a derivative problem such as 'derivative of x^2 + 3x', a geometry area problem, a simple probability problem). For these you only need to reach the start of a step-by-step session — you do not need to finish them, except as noted below.
8. To create the data needed for the Review Notebook and Learning History checks: complete at least TWO problems end-to-end (the anchor '2x + 5 = 13' plus one more, and make sure at least one of them contains a wrong step response), and make sure the Review Notebook ends up holding records of at least two different problem types (e.g. one algebra/linear-equation record and one geometry record) by answering a step incorrectly in a geometry problem too. Use distinct, easily recognisable problem texts so records can be told apart later.
9. Review Notebook: open a record's detail to inspect its contents; then use the search field with a keyword that appears in only one record, and separately apply the problem-type filter for one type, observing the list before and after each action. Clear the search/filter between the two checks.
10. Learning History: visit it only after the above sessions are finished. Before reading the page, write down from your own log how many problems you completed and how many step responses were correct versus incorrect, then compare those with the figures the page shows (completed count, accuracy, frequently missed concepts, recent progress).
11. Persistence: perform the page reload only at the very end, after all data has been created. After reloading, re-open the solved-problem record/history and the Review Notebook and confirm the previously observed problem text, solution path, mistaken step and correct solution are still present. Do not use a refresh as a substitute for any other check.
12. Stability notes: AI-backed actions (recognition, hints, follow-up answers, practice generation) can take several seconds — wait for the loading/typing indicator to finish before capturing, and retry once if a request visibly errors. Record the visual impression of the home page and the solving view (background, accent colours, formula-card styling) while you are already on those pages, not from memory.

title: Human Anatomy Explorer
query: Build a web app called Human Anatomy Explorer for students who want to learn anatomy visually. Center the home page on interactive 3D organ models, with a library containing the heart, brain, lungs, liver, kidneys, eyes, intestines, pancreas, and skin. After choosing an organ, users can drag to rotate it, zoom in and out, isolate it, view it in layers, and open a cross-section. Mark important structures with clickable labels. For example, selecting the aorta, atrium, or ventricle on the heart should open a panel with the structure’s name, location, and function. Each organ’s learning page should cover its size, location, main functions, blood supply, tissue structure, and common conditions, with microscopic tissue views, side-by-side organ comparisons, and simple functional animations. Add a Blood Circulation mode that begins at the heart and animates the direction of blood through the atria, ventricles, lungs, and major vessels. Use different colors and moving particles to distinguish oxygenated and deoxygenated blood. Users can pause at any stage to see where the blood is, what is happening, and where it goes next. Include an interactive study mode that asks students to find a randomly selected structure on the 3D model. A correct choice highlights the structure and explains its role; a wrong choice reveals the correct location. After completing an organ, record progress and accuracy and let students bookmark structures they tend to confuse. Use a warm off-white background, medical illustrations, specimen-style labels, and soft organ colors. It should feel like a digital anatomy atlas that can be rotated, taken apart, and explored—not a traditional textbook.

verification_guideline:
Verification order and stabilization notes for "Human Anatomy Explorer":

- Start on the home page and first inventory the organ library (heart, brain, lungs, liver, kidneys, eyes, intestines, pancreas, skin). Record which entries exist and which open a working detail/learning view, since almost every later step depends on successfully entering an organ view.
- Use the heart as the primary organ for the full interaction pass (it is the organ named in the requirements for labels and circulation). Only after the heart pass, spot-check one or two other organs (e.g., brain or lungs) to see whether the same viewer features are organ-specific or shared.
- For the 3D viewer, exercise the manipulations one at a time and take a screenshot before and after each so the state change is visible: (1) press and drag across the model area to rotate (a click alone is not a drag — press, move a noticeable distance, then release), (2) zoom in and out (try scroll wheel over the model and any on-screen zoom controls/buttons), (3) isolate, (4) layer view / layer switching, (5) cross-section. If the model is rendered in a canvas, allow a few seconds for it to load before interacting, and re-check whether controls are on-canvas, in a side toolbar, or in a menu before concluding a control is absent.
- Structure labels: click a visible label/hotspot on the model (e.g., aorta, atrium, ventricle) and read the opened panel for the structure name, location, and function. Try at least two different structures to confirm the panel content changes per structure rather than being static.
- Learning page content (size, location, main functions, blood supply, tissue structure, common conditions), microscopic tissue view, side-by-side organ comparison, and functional animation may live in separate tabs/sections of the organ page — scroll the whole page and open every tab before judging any of these as missing. For comparison, actually select the two organs being compared if a selector is offered.
- Blood Circulation mode: enter it, let the animation run for several seconds to observe particle motion and the color distinction between oxygenated and deoxygenated blood, then use the pause control and read the stage information (current location, what is happening, where blood goes next). Also try stepping/advancing between stages if such controls exist. If an animation is long or loops slowly, use advance_time only after the animation has actually started.
- Study mode: it depends on entering an organ and its quiz being started. Deliberately perform BOTH outcomes in separate rounds — first answer a prompted structure correctly (observe highlight + explanation), then in another round deliberately choose a wrong structure (observe whether the correct location is revealed). Note the prompted structure text each round so you can tell whether the target is randomized across rounds.
- Progress and accuracy tracking: before answering any question, look at the progress/statistics area and note the initial (possibly zero/empty) values; a clean empty state is not evidence of missing functionality. Then complete several questions for one organ and re-check that the recorded progress/accuracy reflects the answers you actually gave. Note the exact numbers you saw so you can compare them with your own count of correct/incorrect answers.
- Bookmarks for confusing structures: bookmark a specific, identifiable structure (record its exact name), then navigate away to another page/tab (e.g., home page or a different organ) and return to the bookmark list to check the same named entry is still there. A page refresh may be used only to test persistence, not as a substitute for observing in-app updates.
- Visual style requirements (warm off-white background, medical-illustration look, specimen-style labels, soft organ colors) should be judged from full-page screenshots of the home page and at least one organ page, not from a cropped region.
- If any control appears to do nothing, retry once with a slightly different interaction (e.g., drag from a different point on the model, or use a keyboard/button alternative) and capture screenshots of both attempts before drawing a conclusion, so transient rendering delays are not mistaken for missing behavior.

title: Prepress Imposition Bay
query:
Build Prepress Imposition Bay, a Web App that turns a book or booklet specification into both a press-ready imposition and an explainable customer quotation. Customers enter trim size, page count, quantity, colour mode, binding, inside stock and cover stock, then upload page assets. The production view exposes machine-sheet sizes, material prices, setup charges, spoilage rates, finishing rates and markup; the customer view shows the resulting options and price breakdown.

Preflight every page for effective resolution, bleed, safety margin, RGB content, undeclared spot colours and stock-specific ink coverage. Blocking issues must identify the page, measured value and required limit. Saddle-stitched jobs require page counts divisible by four and calculate creep from sheet depth and paper caliper; perfect-bound jobs calculate spine width from page count, caliper and bulk factor. Render front-and-back sheet diagrams with page numbers, rotations, fold lines and a stepped fold simulation proving the final reading order.

Calculate sheets per copy from the signature, then total sheets including rounded-up setup and spoilage allowances. Separate paper, printing, setup, binding, trimming and packaging costs, showing each formula with substituted values. Apply quantity-based finishing rates and markup to produce total price, unit price and gross margin. Recompute all figures when quantity, stock, binding, machine sheet or imposition changes.

Generate three comparable production options, such as economical stock, fewer signatures or premium binding. Compare price, unit cost, paper use, waste percentage, spine or creep impact and unresolved risks. Never recommend a cheaper option that creates a blocking production violation.

Seed a forty-eight-page saddle-stitch job with low-resolution images, insufficient bleed, an RGB page and a fold-crossing barcode. Produce a printable quotation and production ticket. Reject zero or negative rates, explain quantity breaks, and retain waived warnings with written reasons. Use millimetres to one decimal and a configurable currency; do not process payments.

verification_guideline:
Operate in a fixed order; most checkpoints depend on a loaded job with computed figures.

1) Prepare state first: on entry, look for the seeded/demo 48-page saddle-stitch job trigger (a "load demo/sample job" style entry) and load it before touching anything else. If the app starts empty, an empty state with a visible seed/create entry is not the same as missing functionality — create or load the job first, then re-check the dependent areas.
2) Survey the shell before editing: in the production view, list which rate controls are actually editable (machine-sheet size, material/stock prices, setup charge, spoilage rate, finishing rates, markup). Then switch to the customer view on the SAME loaded job and note what is shown vs. hidden. Switch back to the production view before continuing.
3) Baseline capture (critical for later recompute checks): with the seeded job loaded, write down in one screenshot pass — sheets per copy, total sheets, each cost line and its formula text, total price, unit price, gross margin, creep value, and any mm dimensions. All later parameter-change checks must be compared against these recorded numbers, not against memory.
4) Preflight before parameter edits: run/open the preflight report on the seeded job and scroll through the full per-page list (expand any collapsed sections or per-page detail). Record the page numbers, measured values and stated limits for the low-resolution, insufficient-bleed, RGB and fold-crossing/barcode findings, and confirm all six check categories appear somewhere in the report.
5) Waiver test with unique text: waive one warning (not a blocking issue if the app distinguishes them) using a unique reason string such as "WAIVE-CUA-<HHMM>", then re-open the preflight report and confirm the waived item and that exact string are still listed. Do not rely on default sample reasons.
6) Upload check in isolation: use the page-asset upload control with the provided fixture files. Record the listed/counted page assets before and after the upload so the change is attributable to your action. If uploading into the seeded job would overwrite or extend its 48 pages, prefer creating a new/blank job for the upload test, then return to the seeded job afterwards.
7) One change at a time, then revert: for the recompute checks, change only one parameter (quantity → stock → binding → machine sheet → imposition/signature), observe the recomputed sheets, cost breakdown, price, unit price and margin without reloading the page, then restore the original value before the next change. Reloading the app is only acceptable to confirm persistence, never as a substitute for live recompute.
8) Binding-specific order: verify creep and the front/back sheet diagrams and the stepped fold simulation while the job is still saddle-stitch (step the simulation through every fold step to its final state, not just the first step); only afterwards switch binding to perfect-bound to observe spine width, then switch back to saddle-stitch. Also test the page-count rule by setting a non-multiple-of-four value (e.g. 46) while saddle-stitch is selected, capture the response, then restore 48.
9) Rate validation: enter 0 and then a negative value in one production rate/price field, capture the app's response, and confirm what happened to the previously recorded figures; restore a valid value afterwards so subsequent checks are not run on a broken state.
10) Currency and formatting: change the configured currency and then re-check the price breakdown, total price and unit price in both the production and customer views. For the millimetre-formatting checkpoint, read the actual rendered strings (trim size, bleed, creep, spine, sheet sizes) rather than judging from labels.
11) Printable outputs: trigger the quotation and the production ticket separately. They may open a new tab, an overlay print layout, or a browser print dialog — if a native print dialog appears, dismiss it and inspect the underlying print layout content. Confirm the printed content reflects the current job's values, not placeholder text.
12) Options and payment scan: open the three generated production options and record, per option, every comparison metric shown and any blocked/violation marking plus which option is presented as recommended. Finally scan the quotation, customer view and printable outputs for any pay/checkout control and record the absence or presence explicitly.

title: Palimpsest Atlas
query:
Build Palimpsest Atlas, a Web App for restoring and georeferencing scanned historical maps while preserving uncertainty. Users can create multiple local projects by uploading PNG or JPEG maps; each project may contain one scan or several adjoining sheets. The workspace synchronizes the original scan and rectified result, allowing users to crop, rotate, mask damaged margins, and create paired control points by selecting the same landmark in both views. Each pair displays its residual distance and direction.

Offer affine, projective, and thin-plate-spline transformations. Moving or excluding a control point immediately refits the map and updates displacement vectors, a distortion heatmap, total error, and withheld check-point error. Detect local foldovers where the transform reverses orientation. For mismatched sheets, allow separate transformation zones whose shared boundaries expose alignment and seam scores.

After rectification, users can trace roads, waterways, buildings, boundaries, and labels. Vertices snap to nearby geometry, intersections share nodes, and polygons cannot self-intersect. Every feature records whether it was directly observed, interpolated across damage, or manually reconstructed, together with a confidence level. A lens, opacity slider, and swipe divider compare the scan, transformed image, and vector overlay. If a control-point edit moves traced features beyond a chosen tolerance, require the user to accept the shift, preserve selected coordinates, or review each affected feature; nothing may drift silently.

Include a fictional town map only as a demonstration fixture, with perspective skew, a torn corner, eight control points including one outlier, a poor sheet seam, and partially traced features. Users must also be able to start empty projects with their own maps. Export the rectified raster, GeoJSON features, control-point table, transformation settings, and residual statistics as one package. All processing and project data remain local.
