verification_guideline:
Operating order (follow this skeleton to keep runs comparable):
1) Land on the entry/dashboard screen and note whether a built-in fictional-town demonstration project already exists; open it first and use it as the primary scenario for control-point, transformation, diagnostics, zone/seam, tracing, comparison, drift and export checks, since these all depend on an already-fitted map with control points and partial tracing.
2) Only after finishing the fixture-based checks, return to the dashboard and create at least one empty project from an uploaded map file (see fixtures) to cover project creation, multi-project coexistence, adding an adjoining sheet, and local persistence.

Key dependency notes:
- Control-point residual distance/direction, total error, check-point error, displacement vectors, distortion heatmap and foldover detection are only observable after a transformation has been fitted with control points; if a freshly uploaded empty project shows none of these, first place control points there or go back to the demonstration project rather than concluding the feature is absent.
- Tracing tools, feature provenance/confidence and GeoJSON export require a rectified result to exist first; sheet-zone alignment/seam scores require a project containing more than one sheet or more than one defined zone.
- Drift-control checks require traced features to already exist AND a tolerance value to be configured (set the tolerance low) BEFORE moving a control point; move the control point last and observe what happens before dismissing any dialog. Verify each of the offered resolutions separately, undoing or re-triggering the drift condition between attempts.
- Foldover detection should be attempted only after selecting the thin-plate-spline model, then dragging a single control point a large distance.
- The withheld check-point statistic requires explicitly marking at least one point as a check/withheld point first.

Interaction stability:
- Control-point creation is a two-step cross-view action: click the landmark in one view, then the corresponding landmark in the other view; confirm the pair appears in the table before continuing.
- For dragging (control points, crop rectangle, swipe divider, lens, opacity slider) press, move in several intermediate steps, then release over the target canvas; click the canvas/panel once first so it holds focus. For label features, click the map position and then type the text into whatever input appears and commit it.
- Before and after each numeric-changing action (excluding a point, switching transformation model, moving a point), read and record the displayed total error / residual values so the change can be compared; do not rely on memory of the visual only.
- Take a screenshot immediately after an action that is claimed to be instant (immediate refit, displacement vectors, heatmap update) — do not reload the page, since reloading would mask whether the update was automatic.

Data hygiene:
- Give every project, traced feature and label you create a unique marker (e.g. a short timestamp or suffix such as _t1423) so it can be distinguished from pre-seeded demonstration content when checking feature lists, persistence after reload, and exported files.
- Reloading/re-entering the app is allowed only for the persistence check (projects, uploaded scans, control points, traced features and provenance still present).
- A newly created empty project legitimately shows empty control-point/feature lists; treat an informative empty state as an empty state, not as a missing feature.

Export and runtime:
- Trigger export once from a fitted project that also has traced features, and observe whether one package or several separate files are produced; then inspect the downloaded package contents (file listing / extraction / opening the produced files) to check for the rectified raster, GeoJSON, control-point table, transformation settings and residual statistics, and compare the exported error figures with the values shown on screen.
- Keep the browser console and network activity monitored across the whole session (upload, refit, tracing, comparison tools, export) so error-level logs and any outbound transmission of map/project payloads can be reported at the end.

title: Wall Installation Planning Studio
query:
Build Wall Installation Planning Studio, a Chinese-language Web App for planning picture frames, decorative panels, and other wall-mounted objects. Users enter the wall’s width, height, and measurement unit, then mark doors, windows, electrical outlets, radiators, no-drill zones, and furniture occlusion lines using rectangles or polygons. Each object records its outer dimensions, weight, orientation, number of mounting points, mounting-point coordinates relative to the object, and compatible mounting hardware. The canvas must display everything at true scale and support zooming, panning, rotation, snapping, and precise numeric adjustment. Every drag operation must immediately update the object’s real-world distances from wall edges, neighboring objects, and reference lines.

Divide all conditions into hard constraints and soft preferences. Objects must not overlap or enter restricted areas; mounting points must fall within permitted regions; and mounting hardware must not exceed its load capacity. Optional preferences include equal spacing, axis alignment, keeping the visual center of gravity close to a specified focal point, centering the overall bounding box, and minimizing the number of drilled holes. Users can assign priorities to these conditions and lock selected objects. The solver then generates three substantially different candidate layouts, listing each layout’s score, unmet preferences, and movement cost. If no valid solution exists, the app must return a minimal conflicting set of conditions rather than merely displaying failure, and allow the user to temporarily relax one condition before recalculating.

After selecting a layout, users enter installation verification mode. Using the wall’s bottom-left corner as the origin, the app outputs the horizontal and vertical coordinates of every mounting point, the required hardware type, estimated load, and installation sequence. When the wall dimensions, restricted zones, or any object are modified, recompute only the affected portion and use before-and-after ghost overlays to visualize displacement. Include unit-conversion and rounding-error checks to ensure that converting between centimeters and inches and back never shifts a mounting point by more than one millimeter. Seed the app with an example containing a sloped ceiling, an electrical outlet, and six objects of different weights so collision detection, load limits, object locking, infeasibility explanations, and the installation checklist can all be directly verified. Use a technical drawing aesthetic, and distinguish states with line styles and text labels in addition to color.

verification_guideline:
Operate the app in the order below; many checkpoints depend on earlier steps succeeding, and several steps are destructive to the seeded scene, so keep the destructive ones last.

1. First load, observe only. Before clicking anything, capture the initial state: wall width/height/unit, the presence of a sloped ceiling boundary, the labeled outlet/restricted zones, and the full object list with each object's weight, size, orientation, mounting-point count and hardware. Write these values down — they are the baseline for later comparisons (locking, solver, incremental recompute, unit round-trip). If the app opens empty, look for an entry such as "载入示例/示例场景" and load it before continuing.
2. Do the purely structural/read-only inspections next, while the scene is still pristine: the annotation panel's obstacle-type choices, the add/edit-object form fields, the hard-constraint list and the soft-preference list. Open each panel via its own entry (side panel, tab, or dialog) and scroll it fully — missing items may only be below the fold.
3. Then do non-destructive canvas interactions on the seeded objects: zoom (control or wheel over the canvas), pan (drag empty background or the pan tool), rotate a selected object, enable snapping and drag one object toward another's alignment line, and use the numeric X/Y fields. For any drag, click the object once to select it first, then press-move-release in several intermediate steps so the app registers the drag and updates live readouts; take a screenshot immediately after release, before clicking elsewhere.
4. Whenever a drag/edit changes an object's position, record its original numeric coordinates beforehand and restore them (undo or by typing the original X/Y back) before moving to the next check, so that later solver/installation checks are not polluted by leftover violations.
5. Constraint-violation checks (overlap, intrusion into the outlet/no-drill zone, a mounting point falling in a no-drill zone, hardware overload) should each be produced deliberately and one at a time: move the object, then look for the violation report in whatever surface the app uses (inline badge on the canvas, a validation/conflict panel, or a toast). For the overload case, edit the heaviest object's assigned hardware/rated capacity rather than inventing a new object.
6. For newly created objects use a unique, recognizable name (e.g. "画框A-T1" plus a two-digit marker) so it cannot be confused with seeded sample data, and confirm it appears both in the object list and on the canvas.
7. Solver flow order: set a priority for at least two preferences and lock one seeded object (record its coordinates first), then trigger solve, then inspect the candidate list (count, per-candidate score / unmet preferences / movement cost, and per-object coordinates of each candidate), then apply one candidate and re-read the object coordinates. An empty results area before pressing solve is a normal empty state, not a missing feature.
8. Enter installation verification mode only after a layout has been selected/applied; if the entry is disabled, go back and confirm a candidate is actually selected. In that mode read the full checklist (scroll to the end) for mounting-point coordinates, hardware type, estimated load and sequence numbering, and cross-check them against the object properties you recorded in step 1.
9. title: Surface Lineage Forge
query:
Build Surface Lineage Forge, a Web App for managing a production material library whose parameters are inherited across a directed tree. Seed 24 materials across four levels and 30 scene objects. Each material has a parent, shading model, local parameter values, and procedural texture slots; each object has a material assignment and optional overrides.

For every parameter, resolve the effective value by checking the object override, local material, nearest ancestor, then the shading-model default. Display the winning value, its exact source, and the skipped candidates. Before a parent edit is committed, calculate the affected descendants and objects, show old versus new resolved values, and separate visible changes from values masked by lower overrides.

Detect and explain inheritance cycles, orphaned textures, overrides equal to inherited values, children that override every parent parameter, and parameters invalid for their shading model. Add physical checks for contradictory pairs such as high metalness with high transmission. Each finding must identify the shortest causal path and offer a narrowly scoped repair rather than a generic warning.

Re-parenting must offer two explicit modes: follow the new parent, or preserve appearance by baking only the parameter values that would otherwise change. Preview both outcomes before applying them. If a parent changes shading model, list invalidated descendant parameters and require a keep-inert or discard decision for each affected branch.

Use a three-pane workspace: inheritance tree, resolved-parameter inspector, and synchronized preview sphere/object. Selecting a node highlights every dependent object; filtering to one parameter redraws only the edges through which that value flows. Include an impact matrix comparing candidate edits, deterministic undo/redo, and a validation view summarizing inheritance depth, masked edits, redundant overrides, and unresolved assets. All sample data and calculations run locally.

verification_guideline:
Order of work (later steps depend on earlier ones succeeding; do not skip ahead):
1. First survey the landing state without editing anything: locate the three panes (inheritance tree, resolved-parameter inspector, preview viewport) and any secondary entry points (diagnostics/findings, impact matrix, validation/summary view, undo/redo controls, re-parent action, parameter filter). Record where each lives before mutating data, because several later checks require comparing against the original seeded state.
2. Record the seeded inventory before any edit: count material nodes (expand every collapsed branch of the tree first, since counts are only observable when all levels are visible) and count scene objects in whatever list/panel holds them. Trace at least one root-to-leaf chain and write down its node names and depth. These numbers must be captured before edits, undo/redo, or repairs change them.
3. Read-only resolution checks come before any mutation: select a leaf-level material and note, per parameter, the winning value, its stated source, and any listed skipped candidates. Then pick (a) a scene object that carries overrides, (b) a material with no local value for a parameter that its parent and grandparent both define, and (c) a parameter that appears to fall through to a model default. For each case, note the exact source label wording as shown; do not infer source from the value alone.
4. Only after read-only inspection, perform mutations, and perform them one at a time, re-checking the diagnostics/validation views between actions so that a finding introduced by one edit is not confused with a pre-existing seeded one.
5. Parent-edit impact preview: choose a material that clearly has descendants and at least one descendant/object that overrides the same parameter (identify such a node from the skipped-candidate or override information gathered in step 3). Change the parameter to a distinctly different value (e.g. move a 0-1 slider/field to a far end rather than a nudge) so old vs new values are visually distinguishable. Confirm the tree/inspector state before confirming, then commit, then re-open a non-overriding descendant to observe propagation.
6. Undo/redo: run these immediately after a single, well-recorded commit (parameter edit or re-parent). Note the exact pre-edit resolved value and tree position first, then undo, then redo, checking the same node each time. Avoid stacking multiple edits before testing undo.
7. Re-parenting: initiate re-parent on a material whose current and prospective parents differ in at least one resolved parameter, so the two modes produce different outcomes. Inspect the comparison of both modes and verify the tree is untouched at that point, then apply one mode and inspect the moved material's resolved values and sources. If you want to exercise the second mode, undo or re-parent back first, and re-record the baseline.
8. Cycle detection: attempt a re-parent that targets a node inside the material's own subtree (identify the subtree from the tree pane first). Treat a blocking dialog, an inline error, or a diagnostics entry as the observable result; capture whatever the app reports rather than assuming a specific channel.
9. Diagnostics-triggering edits: for the redundant-override and contradictory-pair checks, first read the value the node would inherit, then set the override to exactly that value; and set metalness and transmission both to high values (e.g. 0.9) on one material. After each such edit, re-open the diagnostics list and note which findings are new. When testing a scoped repair, record the full findings list before applying, apply exactly one finding's repair, then re-read the list and the touched node.
10. Shading-model change: perform this on a material that has descendants carrying parameters the new model does not support; capture any listed invalidated parameters and the per-branch keep-inert/discard decision UI, and complete or cancel the flow deliberately so subsequent checks start from a known state.
11. Filtering and highlighting: use the single-parameter filter and the node-selection highlight as separate observations; before filtering, screenshot the unfiltered graph so the difference in drawn edges is comparable. For highlighting, note both which objects become highlighted and that non-dependent objects do not.
12. Preview synchronization: pick two materials whose resolved base color or roughness clearly differ (use the inspector values recorded earlier to choose) and screenshot the preview for each in the same session.
13. Local execution: keep the network/request log observable across load, resolution, impact preview and re-parent actions; note that absence of an empty diagnostics or empty impact list is not evidence of a missing feature when no qualifying condition exists yet — first create the triggering condition, then re-check.
14. Use recognizable, distinctive values for any edit you make (e.g. an extreme or unusual numeric value) so that later screenshots can attribute a changed resolved value to your own action rather than to seeded data.

title: Roomfolio — An Explorable Personal Room
query:
Build Roomfolio, a Web App that transforms a person’s structured profile into an explorable, one-of-a-kind isometric room that also functions as their personal website. Start with four visually distinct templates—Warm Studio, Minimal Gallery, Pixel Apartment, and Future Lab—then let the creator adjust palette, lighting, material mood, and visual density before generating the room.

The profile editor collects a name, headline, biography, locations, education, work history, projects, skills, achievements, interests, favorite books, and contact links. Photos may be uploaded, cropped, reordered, given alt text, and assigned to projects or milestones. A semantic mapping engine must turn profile entries into meaningful room objects: education may occupy a bookshelf, projects a workbench or computer, travel a wall map, achievements a display cabinet, and hobbies their own instruments or collections. Every object keeps a visible “derived from” link to its source entry, and a coverage panel flags any profile information not represented in the room.

Generate three genuinely different room compositions while respecting wall/floor placement, non-overlap, object scale, depth order, doorway clearance, and a navigable path through the scene. The creator can lock objects, regenerate only the remainder, drag, rotate, resize, swap an object’s visual metaphor, or bind it to a different entry. Editing profile text must update the bound object without destroying its manual placement. Changing templates must translate objects to equivalent assets where possible and present an explicit review list for replacements or unmapped items.

Visitor Mode removes editing controls and turns the room into an interactive narrative. Hovering or focusing reveals subtle hotspots; selecting an object opens a layered card containing the related introduction, dates, timeline entries, links, and image gallery. Provide a guided tour whose order can differ from the chronological timeline, stable deep links to individual objects, and browser back/forward behavior that restores the correct open object and camera position.

Support desktop pan and zoom, mobile touch navigation, keyboard traversal, an accessible object list, reduced-motion mode, and contrast-safe hotspot indicators. Include editor/visitor and desktop/mobile previews. Seed a complete example profile with several related projects, two image galleries, and one intentionally unmapped skill so generation, coverage repair, template switching, object rebinding, history navigation, and responsive behavior can all be verified. Persist the full project locally and export a self-contained static website plus a JSON backup that restores content, bindings, and coordinates exactly.
